None covers this finding. Related: KS-1176.

title: api-gateway limiter: the no-allowance warning throttle is keyed without the tenant, and the jwt:<tenant>:<id> bucket joins two claims with an ambiguous ':'
description:
## BLUF

Two minor findings from the Opus gate on PR #1463 (KS-1205, squash `db0df4540acfcf3fa14a4f7d37d061916f3d5bae`), both in `middleware/rateLimitEnforce.ts`, both small and neither reachable by a real producer today. Plus one rollout note for whoever deploys it.

## Recommendation

One fix, one test pass, both findings: build the bucket and the throttle key from the same encoded parts. Priority Low.

## Detail

1. **The warning throttle is keyed without the tenant** (`rateLimitEnforce.ts:155`, `warnNoAllowance(String(user.connectorId || user.userId), ...)`). Two tenants' principals that share a `connectorId` share one 30-second warning slot, so one tenant's "no rateLimit" warning can hide the other's. It affects logs only. Key the throttle on `clientId` (the bucket), which already carries the tenant.
2. **The** `jwt:<tenant>:<id>` **bucket uses an ambiguous delimiter** (`:92`, `jwtBucket`). Either claim may contain `:`, so tenant `a:b` with id `x` and tenant `a` with id `b:x` both give `jwt:a:b:x` and share one bucket. Reaching it needs the RS256 signing key (the claims are signed), and it stays inside the `jwt:` namespace, so it can never reach an `api_key:` bucket. Encode each part (for example `encodeURIComponent`, or a length prefix) so the join is unambiguous, with a cell for the colliding pair.
3. **Rollout note (no fix):** during a rolling deploy, old and new pods count machine-JWT principals under different Redis keys (`ratelimit:<id>` against `ratelimit:jwt:<tenant>:<id>`), so such a principal can briefly be allowed up to twice its allowance for the rollout plus one window. API-key buckets do not change. There is no production producer of a machine JWT by READ, so this is for the deploy seat to know, not to act on.

## Source and dedupe

* The Opus gate on PR #1463, 2026-10-12, defects 1 and 2 and note N2 (`WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-10-12_gate-pr1463/verdict.md`); line numbers re-read at develop `db0df4540acf`.
* **Not filed here:** the gateway `tsc` configuration skipping test files (30 existing errors, none in KS-1205's files) is KS-1090's subject; the measurement is a comment there.
* **Searched first** (Linear, includeArchived, literal title/description): `skips test files` 0, `warn throttle` 0, `rolling deploy` 0, `jwt:` 2 (neither about this). Nearest: KS-1156 (the machine-method set and the `oauth` label), a different finding.

Related: KS-1205, KS-1156.

title: api-gateway: every per-IP limiter keys on the last X-Forwarded-For hop (trust proxy 1), so a caller that reaches the gateway without nginx rotates that hop and gets a fresh bucket each request
description:
## BLUF

`index.ts:108` sets `app.set('trust proxy', 1)`, so every IP-keyed control in the gateway (the global limiter at 300 per minute, the verification limiter, the login limiters, the brute-force guard) keys on the **last** `X-Forwarded-For` hop. The Opus gate on PR #1483 (KS-1479) **reproduced against the gateway directly** that rotating that last hop gets a fresh bucket each time, identically on base and on #1483, so the per-IP bound is only as strong as who can set the last hop. Pre-existing, not caused by KS-1479. **Whether it is reachable in practice depends on whether anything reaches the gateway without nginx appending the hop; that part is unmeasured.**

## What the repo's own configs say (READ, not measured)

* `docker/nginx-gateway/nginx.conf:133`, `nginx-production.conf:296` and `nginx-demo.conf:334` all set `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for`, which **appends** nginx's `$remote_addr` to whatever the client sent. Through that nginx, the last hop is the address nginx saw (and on demo, `nginx-demo.conf:100-107` resolves it from `X-Forwarded-For` only for trusted source addresses with `real_ip_recursive on`). A client behind it can prepend hops but cannot choose the last one.
* The gate's reproduction sent the header **straight to the gateway**, with no nginx in front. So the exposure is any path that reaches the gateway without that nginx: a published gateway port, another container on the compose network (the comment at `nginx-demo.conf:89` already names this for nginx's own rate limit), or an ingress that passes the header through.
* The related finding on how the IP is derived at all is **KS-618** (archived, Backlog, P2): on demo every IP-keyed control saw the Docker bridge address because two proxy hops met `trust proxy 1`; its recommended fix (an explicit trusted-subnet list rather than a hop count) is also the fix shape here. Its nginx realip half appears to be in `nginx-demo.conf` now; whether it is deployed on demo and Kintsugi is not known to me.

## Recommendation

1. **Measure first, read-only, after the Kintsugi window:** through the real public front door, send several `GET /api/credentials/abc` (answered 401 by the gateway's own gate, after the global limiter) with different client-supplied `X-Forwarded-For` first hops and read the `RateLimit-Remaining` header each time. If it keeps decrementing across them they share one bucket (the edge fixes the hop); if it resets, the hop is client-controlled at the real ingress. This needs no credential and writes nothing but limiter counters. Also check the compose files and VM firewalls for any published gateway port.
2. **If any path reaches the gateway without nginx:** replace the hop count with an explicit trusted-proxy list (KS-618's recommendation), so `X-Forwarded-For` is honoured only from the nginx peer.
3. Add a cell that sends a forged last hop to the real app with `trust proxy` configured as intended. Priority P2 as Wednesday ruled; it may drop to P3 if step 1 shows the edge appends the hop.

## Detail

* Source: the Opus gate on PR #1483, 2026-10-12, note N3 and its XFF probe (`WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-10-12_gate-pr1483/verdict.md`, `evidence/`): "the key is the last hop; rotating the last hop bypasses the limit, as on develop; rotating the first hop with the last fixed does not". Edge configuration was not checked by the gate.
* **Searched first** (Linear, includeArchived, literal title and description): `X-Forwarded-For`, `trust proxy`, `last hop`, `XFF`, `x-real-ip`, `set_real_ip_from`, `spoof`: nearest is KS-618 (above); nothing covers a client-chosen last hop.

Related: KS-618, KS-1479, KS-946, KS-1469.

title: api-gateway: /api/v1/v2/verification/* is rewritten to the v2 verify route but matches none of the three per-IP verification limiter mounts
description:
## BLUF

`/api/v1/v2/verification/*` is a spelling the gateway rewrites to the **v2** verify route (the `/api/v1/` strip in `index.ts`), but it matches **none of the three** per-IP verification limiter mounts (`/api/verification`, `/api/v1/verification`, `/api/v2/verification`) added by KS-1469, because the limiter runs before the rewrite and sees `/api/v1/v2/...`. Measured by the Opus gate on PR #1472 with the verification cap at 3: **NODE_ENV=test: 5 of 5 get through, production: 6 of 6**, all reaching the upstream; it is counted only by the global limiter (300 per minute per IP, measured by the gate in a production boot). Pre-existing, not a regression: before KS-1469 none of the v1 spellings was counted. It is an inconsistency inside KS-1469 itself: the same PR's CSRF change treats this spelling as an alias.

## Recommendation

One small PR, tests first, built after KS-1457. The gate measured a fix that works: **one limiter instance placed AFTER the** `/api/v1/` **rewrite, on** `['/api/verification', '/api/v2/verification']`; it passed all 31 KS-1469 cells (including the production-boot 307 cell) and the gate's own three cells for this spelling. Because the rewrite has already turned every `/api/v1/...` spelling into the plain path by then, the `/api/v1/verification` mount becomes redundant. Re-run the production cell and re-check that a followed 307 is still counted once, and that the unversioned production 307s staying uncounted (a trade-off KS-1469's PR states) is unchanged. Priority P3.

## Detail

* Source: the Opus gate on PR #1472 (KS-1469), 2026-10-12, defect 1 (`WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-10-12_gate-pr1472/verdict.md`; its probe cells G1 red on head, G2 and G3 green).
* **Searched first** (Linear, includeArchived, literal title and description): `v1/v2/verification`, `v2/verification`: nothing tracks this spelling.
* Not checked by the gate: whether originate actually serves `/api/v1/...` paths (HPM 2.0.10 forwards `originalUrl`, and originate mounts only the unversioned and v2 paths: by reading, unmeasured).

Related: KS-1469, KS-946, KS-1461.

title: pre-push resolves the bare name `develop`, so a TAG named develop beats the branch — and --quiet suppresses the ambiguity warning
description:
## BLUF

`git rev-parse --verify --quiet develop` **resolves a TAG named** `develop` **in preference to the branch, and** `--quiet` **suppresses the ambiguity warning that would otherwise say so. The hook would then compute its base against the tag.** Latent, not live: `git tag -l develop` is empty in this repo today.

## Where

`.githooks/pre-push:98–99` — the loop's first candidate is the bare name `develop`, verified with `git rev-parse --verify --quiet "$_ref"`.

## Measured (git 2.51.0, isolated fixture)

Three commits c1/c2/c3; a tag `develop` at c1, a branch `develop` at c2, `HEAD` at c3.

```
SCENARIO A — tag develop, NO branch develop
  git rev-parse --verify --quiet develop  -> b02eae510   (THE TAG)
  the loop breaks on it and uses it as the base: YES

SCENARIO B — BOTH a tag (c1) and a branch (c2)
  git rev-parse --verify --quiet develop  -> b02eae510   (THE TAG)
  git rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/heads/develop -> 621667116   (the branch)

ambiguity warning
  with --quiet : 0
  without      : 1            <- the control: the warning exists, --quiet is what hides it

consequence
  git merge-base develop HEAD            -> b02eae510
  git merge-base refs/heads/develop HEAD -> 621667116
```

Two different bases, so two different `changed` sets — and with the warning suppressed there is no signal which ref was used.

## Fix shape

Iterate fully-qualified refs — `refs/heads/develop`, `refs/remotes/origin/develop` — so the name cannot be captured by a tag. This also composes with the fix for the sibling ordering defect (KS-882), which changes which of those two is tried first.

## Regression

A fixture carrying a tag named `develop` at a different commit from the branch must still resolve the base to the branch.

Residue of the #855 tier-2 gate (F-4, Polish). Parent: KS-854, merged at `f72c9023f6e5ca5ca035c0734282d91775533a17`.

title: api-gateway front door: a trailing slash skips the spec method and auth gate, the CSRF exclusions and the per-IP verification limiter miss the /api/v1/ alias, and the v2 verify-batch exclusion is unpinned
description:
## BLUF

The Opus gate on PR #1466 (KS-1461) measured four gaps on base that the PR did not cause. **I reproduced all three runtime ones in my own harness on develop** `b4a245fba1ca` **(which contains #1466), on the real app over real HTTP, with a recording stub for every upstream.** O1 is the one that matters: **a trailing slash skips the gateway's spec method and auth gate.**

|  | canonical | variant | reading |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| **O1** unauthenticated `GET` of a `bearerAuth` operation | `/api/credentials/abc` → **401**, 0 upstream hits | `/api/credentials/abc/` → **200, 1 hit** (also `/API/credentials/abc/`, `/api/v1/credentials/abc/`, `//` at the end) | gate skipped |
| **O1** method gate | `DELETE /api/auth/login` → **405**, 0 hits; `PUT` → 405 | `DELETE /api/auth/login/` → **200, 1 hit**; `PUT` → 200, 1 hit | gate skipped |
| **O3** per-IP verification limiter, cap lowered to 3 | `/api/verification/verify` ×5 → `200,200,200,429,429`; `/api/v2/verification/verify` ×5 → same | `/api/v1/verification/verify` ×5 → `200,200,200,200,200` | not counted |
| **O2** `POST` with a cookie and no token (`NODE_ENV=development`) | `/api/auth/login` → 200; `/api/verification/verify` → 200 | `/api/v1/auth/login` → **403 CSRF_TOKEN_MISSING**; `/api/v1/verification/verify` → **403** | alias not excluded |

Controls in the same run: `/api/zzz-not-in-spec/` → 404 with 0 hits (the gate has no opinion on a path outside the spec, as designed); the canonical v1 requests sent first did not consume the canonical allowance (the canonical five came back `200,200,200,429,429` after them), so the v1 requests really are uncounted rather than counted somewhere else.

**What this does and does not show.** The gateway's own gate is skipped, so the request reaches the upstream. I did **not** measure whether the real upstream or the per-route `authenticateToken` then refuses it (the stub answers 200), so this is a skipped layer, not a measured data exposure. I rate it High on the instruction that O1 is High once reproduced; the per-route check is the only thing standing between the variant and the upstream.

## Recommendation

One ticket, one PR, tests first, built next (ahead of KS-1464 and KS-1457, as the same front-door class):

* **O1** — the spec route regexes are anchored `^…$` while Express routing is non-strict, so `/x/` is routed as `/x`. Let the spec match tolerate one trailing `/`, and pin it with canonical-vs-variant parity cells (GET 401, DELETE 405, in `/api/`, `/API/` and `/api/v1/` spellings) plus the not-in-spec control.
* **O3** — mount the verification limiter on `/api/v1/verification` too. It sits above the `/api/v1/` rewrite in `index.ts`, so the alias is a third spelling it never sees. By code reading (not measured in a production boot) the alias is then counted only by the global limiter, 300 per minute per IP in production, against the dedicated 60: five times looser, not unlimited.
* **O2** — the exclusion list answers for `/api/x` but not for `/api/v1/x`, though the alias is the same route by definition. Make the exclusion check judge the path the alias gives it. **This overlaps KS-1177**, which waits on an owner decision about the v1/v2 verify difference in production; the alias-equivalence reading widens nothing beyond what the canonical spelling already has, but KS-1177's owner should see it.
* **m1** — `csrf.ts` carries a `/api/v2/verification/verify-batch` exclusion that nothing pins (deleting it keeps all 936 tests green), and no live route exists at it in v1 or v2. Either a cell that pins it, or drop both verify-batch entries; decide on evidence (does the spec or the proxy declare the route?).

## Detail

* Source: the Opus gate on PR #1466, 2026-10-12 (`WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-10-12_gate-pr1466/verdict.md`, findings O1, O2, O3 and m1; its probe file is in the same folder). Reproduction here is independent of the gate's: my own harness, on the merged tree.
* The gate measured all four on base and on the merged tree identically, so none is caused by #1466 (squash `c78c13d5f2eb6a8c840e7bc75bdb4a054ffd5d7e`).
* Production note for O2: the production-only 307 sends `/api/x` to `/api/v1/x`, so a cookie-bearing browser call to an excluded path may meet the 403 on the re-POST. The gate did not measure this in production and neither did I.
* **Searched first** (Linear, includeArchived, literal title and description): `trailing slash` (KS-519, 548, 861, 1016: none about the gateway gate), `verification limiter`, `api/v1/verification`, `spec auth gate`, `specRouteMap`, `CSRF exclusion`, `verify-batch`. Nearest: **KS-1177** (O2 on the verify family, Backlog), **KS-946** (limiter spelling class: its eight mounts do not name `/api/v1/verification`), **KS-1358** (405 before authentication), **KS-1165** (Done: the v2 CSRF entries).

Related: KS-1461, KS-801, KS-1177, KS-946, KS-1165.

title: Four path spellings dodge EVERY path-scoped gateway limiter — a CLASS across all eight mounts; first act is the booted-stack experiment
description:
> ## ✅ THE EXPERIMENT IS DONE — re-priced **P1 → P3** on this ticket's own instruction ("re-price it once the experiment answers"). The block below reflects the pre-experiment state; the answer is here.
>
> **This ticket set its own rule:** *"If auth 404s them, F5 is a curio. If auth serves them, F5 is a Blocker on the whole limiter layer, not just MFA."*
>
> **Measured: auth 404s THREE of the four. It serves the fourth — and the fourth is the one** [KS-858](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-858) **already closed** in [#884](<https://github.com/Secuura/Distributed_Secuura/pull/884>), merged, on `develop` and on the demo `400517aaf`. **Three curios and one real dodge, already fixed.**
>
> `POST /api/auth/login` — one of the eight limiter mounts this ticket names — nonexistent address so no real account accrues a lockout counter, `--path-as-is` throughout (without it curl normalises the spellings itself and the run measures nothing):
>
> | path | status | reading |
> | -- | -- | -- |
> | `/api/auth/login` | **401** | canonical **positive control** — reached the backend |
> | `/api/auth//login` | **401** | **SERVED** — the dodge completes |
> | `/api/auth/%6Cogin` | **404** | not routed |
> | `/api/auth/login;x=1` | **404** | not routed |
> | `/api/auth%2Flogin` | **404** | not routed |
> | `/api/auth/zzz-not-a-route` | **404** | negative control |
> | `/api/zzz/login` | **404** | negative control, different prefix |
>
> **Replicated on a second route and method** — authenticated `GET /api/users/me`: canonical **200**, `//me` **200**, `%6De` / `me;x=1` / `%2Fme` all **404**, two negative controls **404**. Two routes, two methods, one partition.
>
> **⚠ THE CAVEAT THAT MAKES THIS TABLE EVIDENCE:** the local stack was created `2026-09-05T00:16:55Z` and **predates KS-858's commits (2026-09-07)**. These are **pre-fix** readings — which is precisely why the `//` row still shows the dodge **live**, rather than being a tautology about an already-patched gateway.
>
> **It also converts an assertion in KS-858's own test into a measurement** — that test declines to handle `%2F`/`%XX`/matrix params on the stated grounds that *"those are 404d by the backend"*. That is now measured, not asserted.
>
> **⚠ DELIBERATELY NOT RUN — and this is an instrument choice, not a gap.** `POST /api/users/me/mfa/disable` was not driven in any spelling. GET cannot discriminate there (the negative control also 404s, so a 404 cannot be separated from "method not routed"), and POST is side-effecting: per [KS-732](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-732) that endpoint does not verify the password it requires, so a successful call **disables MFA on a seeded account**. `login` is the same class — a limiter mount, a POST, a real backend — and answers the question without the side effect.
>
> **⚠ TWO INSTRUMENT FAILURES ON THE WAY TO THAT TABLE, BOTH CAUGHT ONLY BY CONTROLS.** (1) An unauthenticated probe returned **401 for every spelling including the negative control** — the `/api/users/me` catch-all rejects everything under it before routing resolves, so 401 carried no information. Read without the control, that table says *"all four spellings are served"* — the exact opposite of the truth, and it would have re-confirmed this ticket as a Blocker. (2) The first token extraction wrapped the JWT in quotes (858 → 860 chars), so the **canonical** control 401'd and nothing under it meant anything.
>
> **The bound is lifted, not merely stated.** This ticket notes *"KS-733's fix is exactly as bypassable as the twin it achieves parity with."* The one bypass that worked is now closed app-wide at the gateway edge, above every predicate — so KS-733's limiters and their twin both sit behind it.
>
> *Measured by s150, 2026-09-08. Locally booted stack only; the demo box was not touched.*

---

**Four path spellings dodge EVERY path-scoped rate limiter at the gateway.** This is a class across all **eight** mounts, not a defect of any one of them.

## ⚠️ FIRST ACT IS AN EXPERIMENT, NOT A FIX

**Severity is set by the result, not before it.** The decisive half of this finding is unmeasured, and the tester said so plainly:

> *"If auth 404s them, F5 is a curio. If auth serves them, F5 is a Blocker on the whole limiter layer, not just MFA."*

Nothing was booted, so **whether** `createProxyMiddleware` **forwards these spellings, and whether the auth service actually serves** `//mfa/disable`**, is unknown.**

**The experiment:** a locally booted gateway + auth (own copy — **never the demo box**), drive the four spellings, and record for each whether the request *completes at the auth service*, with a canonical-spelling control in the same batch so a uniform failure is distinguishable from a dodge. Filed **P1 on the ruling**; re-price it once the experiment answers.

## The spellings

```
/api/users/me//mfa/disable
/api/users/me/%6Dfa/disable
/api/users/me/mfa;x=1/disable
/api/users/me/mfa%2Fdisable
```

## Mechanism — re-verified here at `066cff675` / #877's head

Two independent layers each decline to act:

1. **The path-scoped limiters are prefix matches.** None of the spellings matches the mount string, so `express-rate-limit` never runs.
2. **The spec-aware gate falls through by design** — `services/api-gateway/src/index.ts:1047`:

   ```js
   const { matched, methods, authedMethods, specPath } = resolveSpecRoute(specMethodMap, req.path);
   if (!matched) return next();
   ```

   An unspecced spelling is passed on, which is documented behaviour and correct in isolation.

Driven by the tester: after exhausting the canonical spelling to **429**, `//mfa/disable` returned **200** — and **express's own prefix strip normalised the dodge away *after* the limiter had already been skipped.** That ordering is the whole defect: the string is abnormal exactly long enough to miss the guard, then becomes normal again in time to be served.

Downstream route confirmed: `routes/proxy.ts:327` — `router.use('/api/users/me', authenticateToken(true), proxy('auth', …))`.

## Scope — all eight mounts, including the one just added

`index.ts` `:939` login · `:951` register · `:958` forgot-password · `:965` refresh · `:972` password-reset · `:979` verify-email · `:986` `/api/auth/mfa` · `:1011` `/api/users/me/mfa`.

**So KS-733's fix is exactly as bypassable as the twin it achieves parity with.** That is not an argument against it — parity was the goal and parity was delivered — but it bounds what was closed, and the bound belongs on KS-733 rather than being discovered later.

## ⚠️ WHAT THE REMEDY MUST NOT BE — this is measured, and it constrains the fix

**A double slash on its own does nothing.** Measured on the real booted gateway, in the same batch as the positive rows:

```
/api/nosuch//thing   -> 404, nothing forwarded
/api/auth//login     -> 200, forwarded as /api/auth/login
```

So this is **not** "double slashes are magic". It is the interaction between an extra slash and a **real mounted prefix**, whose strip normalises the path *after* the limiter has already been passed. The abnormal spelling exists only for the length of the limiter check.

**Consequence for the remedy:** a rule that rejects or collapses `//` platform-wide would be treating the symptom, and it carries its own blast radius — every client that has ever built a URL by concatenation starts getting 400s, and a normaliser placed in front of a security gate is exactly where path-confusion vulnerabilities live. The defect is in **where normalisation happens relative to the guard**, not in the character.

## Fix shape — deliberately not chosen yet

Normalising the path *before* the limiters is the obvious candidate, but normalisation ahead of a security gate is its own hazard class and the experiment may show the requests never complete anyway. **Do not pick a remedy before the measurement.**

*Split from the KS-733 (#877) tier-1 verdict F5, 2026-09-06. Not a defect of that PR. Filed P1 on Wednesday's ruling; the mechanism above was re-verified in this seat rather than taken from the relay.*

title: Audit log records the caller's spelling: case splits the action namespace, /API/ is unaudited, unrouted 404s put caller text in action (KS-871 gate R-4)
description:
## BLUF

The api-gateway audit log writes `action` and `details.path` from the request's own spelling of the path. It never folds case, and never normalises spelling variants of a route. So the same logical route can appear under several action names, some requests are not audited at all, and caller-chosen text reaches the `action` column. This is pre-existing: it is identical on base and on the merged KS-871 fix. It was recorded as R-4 by both QA gate rounds on PR #1011 (KS-871, merged `523f283c6cd2550263ec9869dc5ee722be40df4e`), which widened it in round 2.

Measured on the real app in test and production mode:

* **Case splits the action namespace:**
  * `POST /api/GDPR/erasures` (refused 403) → `GDPR.create`.
  * `POST /api/LOGS` (204) → `LOGS.create`.
  * `POST /api/gdpr/ERASURES` → `gdpr.create`, but `details.path` keeps `/api/gdpr/ERASURES`.
* **An upper-case** `/API/` **prefix is not audited at all:** `POST /API/logs` (204) and `POST /API/GDPR/ERASURES` (403) write no row. The middleware's `/api/` prefix check is case-sensitive.
* **Unrouted 404s put caller text into** `action`**,** identically on base and head:
  * `qa-attacker-chosen.create`, `%6cogs.create`, `logs;x=1.create`, `..create`;
  * `V1.create` and `v1.create` (`/api/v1/v1/logs`, a bare `/api/v1`);
  * `unknown.create` at `/api/` (`/api/v1/`).

## Recommendation

Not built; Backlog. This is a design decision for the audit trail's owner, not a one-line fix. Two choices:

1. **Normalisation:** should the audited path be case-folded, and should dot-segment, `;param` and percent-encoded spellings be normalised before `deriveAction`? Or should the raw spelling be kept in `details.path` and only the `action` be normalised?
2. **Unrouted requests:** should a 404 write a fixed action (e.g. `unrouted.create`) rather than one built from caller text?

Before deciding, check which spellings the edge (nginx / Caddy / Container Apps) actually forwards. The gates marked that NOT TESTED, and it sets how reachable each row above is in a deployment.

## Detail

**Source:**

* Round-2 gate report: `Testing Agent MAIN/projects/secuura/reports/2026-09-17-ks871-1011-6dc825644-tier1-r2/report.md` (carry-forward table, Item 2, Item 3 (ii), Merge-seat ADDENDUM R-4).
* Round-1 report: `…/2026-09-17-ks871-1011-0a1f8900c-tier1-r1/report.md` (Records, R-4).

**Code at develop** `523f283c6` (`services/api-gateway/src/middleware/audit.ts`):

* the middleware returns early unless `req.path.startsWith('/api/')`;
* `deriveAction(req, path)` splits `path` on `/` and builds `<segment>.<verb>` with no case folding.

**Not in this ticket:** the gate also measured routed spelling variants (dot-segment, `;param`, percent-encoded) that keep the caller's text in `details.path` / `action`. Those examples are not reproduced here; Wednesday holds them.

**Not tested by either gate:**

* request-target rewriting at the edge;
* out-of-repo consumers that group rows by `action`.

### Dedupe before filing

Searched with the board's `searchIssues` (includeArchived, includeComments), keeping only literal, case-insensitive matches:

* `GDPR.create`: 92 fuzzy, 1 literal (KS-871 comments).
* `LOGS.create`: 116 fuzzy, 2 literal (KS-5 archived, unrelated; KS-871 comments).
* `unaudited`: 8 fuzzy, 4 literal (KS-903, PS-726, PS-536, KS-229; none about the gateway audit middleware).
* `case-split`: 125 fuzzy, 0 literal.
* `deriveAction`: 2 fuzzy, 2 literal (KS-871; KS-1189, which carries R-3 and R-5 but not R-4).

title: Audit log (KS-871 gate R-3/R-5): H29 attemptedEmail is never written for proxied logins; production rows are v1.* on base and #1011 round 2 changes them
description:
## BLUF

Two pre-existing audit-log gaps, recorded by the tier-1 QA gate on PR #1011 (KS-871) round 1 as R-3 and R-5. Both were re-read against #1011's round-2 head `6dc8256448b50de6a15519001a4f7032ace1ae19`. Neither is built.

* **R-3: H29** `attemptedEmail` **is never written for a login through the gateway.**
  * The audit middleware reads the email from `req.body`. The gateway does not parse bodies on `/api/auth` (a proxied prefix), so the field is absent from every login audit row, on base and on round-1 head, in test and in production mode.
  * #1011 round 2 does not change this (READ).
  * The other half of R-3: on base, a login refused 429 by the login rate limiter is audited as `unknown.create` with path `/`. The gate MEASURED its D3 shape writing `auth.login` / `/api/auth/login` instead. Round 2 uses that shape, so this half moves if #1011 merges (not measured at `6dc825644` itself).
* **R-5: in production mode the audit trail on base already spells mounted and proxied routes** `v1.*`**.**
  * In production mode (`NODE_ENV=production`) the gateway answers the measured `/api/...` writes with a 307 to their `/api/v1/...` spelling. So `v1.login` / `/api/v1/auth/login` is written where a canonical row would be `auth.login` / `/api/auth/login`.
  * **#1011 round 2 changes these rows.** It captures the canonical path at entry, which is the gate's D3 shape, and the gate measured D3 turning those production rows canonical.
  * If #1011 merges, production audit rows change spelling. Anything reading `v1.*` action names would see the change.

## Recommendation

Not built; Backlog. Two things for the owner, neither a fix decided here:

1. **R-3 (H29):** decide whether the attempted-email capture should work at all for proxied logins, and where the email should come from. Today the code expects a parsed body that the gateway deliberately does not parse on `/api/auth`.
2. **R-5:** before or when #1011 merges, check whether anything outside the repo reads audit `action` values. The gate did not test this (its NOT TESTED item 6: "the blast radius of `v1.*` actions is argued, not measured"). Candidates are the security service's audit reader, dashboards and any SIEM export. If nothing depends on `v1.*`, R-5 needs no work.

## Detail

**Source:** gate report `Testing Agent MAIN/projects/secuura/reports/2026-09-17-ks871-1011-0a1f8900c-tier1-r1/report.md` (section Records, R-3 and R-5). The census covered 1115 requests over 119 audited routes on the real app with an in-memory sink, in test and production modes. The D3 comparison is `evidence/compare_production_base_d3.out`.

### R-3: H29 `attemptedEmail`

* `services/api-gateway/src/middleware/audit.ts` at round-2 head `6dc825644` (unchanged from develop `e0f41a8fa` on these lines):
  * `:287-291` sets `attemptedEmail` only when `req.path === '/api/auth/login' && req.body && typeof req.body === 'object'`.
* `services/api-gateway/src/index.ts` at develop `e0f41a8fa`:
  * `:400-404` `proxyPaths` includes `'/api/auth'`;
  * `:413` `shouldParseBody` returns false for those prefixes;
  * `:416` the JSON body parser runs only when `shouldParseBody` is true.
  * So `req.body` is never populated for a proxied login.
* **Measured by the gate:** `details.attemptedEmail` absent on 7 + 3 login rows, for every login spelling, on every tree, in both modes.
* **Unchanged by round 2 (READ):** round 2's `audit.ts` diff touches `deriveAction`'s path source and `details.path` only. The two other finish-time `req.path` reads, the login user-id extraction (`:261`) and the warning-log path (`:333`), are also untouched.
* **The 429 half.** Production mode, same client IP, requests 5 to 7 answered 429 by the login rate limiter:

| Tree | Audit row for a 429 login |
| -- | -- |
| Base | `unknown.create`, resource type `unknown`, path `/`, success false |
| Round-1 head | `auth.login` (test mode) / `v1.login` (production mode) |
| Gate's D3 shape | `auth.login`, resource type `session`, path `/api/auth/login`, success false |

### R-5: the production trail is `v1.*` on base

* **Gate record:** in production mode, 441 base rows equal round-1 head rows and differ from D3, for proxied and mounted admitted routes (`v1.login`, `v1.upload`, `v1.erasures` and so on).
* Example from `compare_production_base_d3.out`, a proxied login answered 200:
  * base: `v1.login`, resource type `v1`, path `/api/v1/auth/login`
  * D3: `auth.login`, resource type `session`, path `/api/auth/login`
* **Re-read against round 2:** `audit.ts` at `6dc825644` vs its merge-base `1125607e9`:
  * `:224` `const auditPath = req.path;` is captured when the middleware runs. It is mounted at the app root after the `/api/v1` strip (`index.ts:570`).
  * That value feeds `deriveAction(req, auditPath)` (`:244`) and `details.path` (`:294`).
  * These are the same two uses as the gate's D3 counterfactual edit (`evidence/d3_apply.py`). So R-5's "a canonical-path fix changes production rows too" now describes #1011 round 2 itself.
  * MEASURED on D3; READ-equivalent for round 2; NOT measured at `6dc825644` (its round-2 gate was being drafted when this was filed).
* develop `e0f41a8fa`'s `audit.ts` is byte-identical to `1125607e9`'s (`git diff --quiet` rc 0), so "base" above is current develop.

### Dedupe before filing

Searched with the board's `searchIssues` (includeArchived, includeComments), keeping only literal, case-insensitive matches in title, description or comments:

* `attemptedEmail`: 1 fuzzy, 1 literal (KS-871, in comments).
* `H29`: 1 fuzzy, 1 literal (KS-871, in comments).
* `middleware/audit.ts`: 101 fuzzy, 3 literal (KS-871; KS-661 and KS-28, both archived and unrelated).
* `v1.`: 105 fuzzy, 35 literal. None is about audit action names; the nearest is KS-1177, a different v1 verify-route defect.

None covers R-3 or R-5. Related: KS-871.

title: api-gateway: more path checks compare the path as sent (the spec method and auth gate, the brute-force login guard, the version prefix), and CSRF exclusions match any prefix
description:
## BLUF

KS-801 (PR #1459, squash `672352369b8ade45d35a7c0e8a9c1656730feaa1`) folded the case of five gateway path predicates. The Opus gate on that PR found **other gateway checks that still compare the path as the client sent it**, and one **pre-existing** CSRF gap. Express routing and every upstream are case insensitive, so `/API/AUTH/LOGIN` reaches the same handler as `/api/auth/login` but may skip these checks. This ticket takes the uncovered ones; the overlapping ones are linked, not re-filed.

## Recommendation

Fold with the same `pathFold.ts` (ASCII only), driven by the same real-HTTP parity matrix, one fix per site. **Do not make routing case sensitive** (measured on KS-801: it turns `403` into `200` on a scope-gated route). Priority is Medium until the first measurement says otherwise; the measurement is the next step, in process, with no login attempts against Kintsugi.

## In scope (READ at develop `672352369b8a`; the measured result goes in a comment)

1. **The spec method and auth gate**, `index.ts:1027`: `if (!req.path.startsWith('/api/')) return next();` is case sensitive, so `/API/...` skips both the `405` method gate and the `401` auth gate. The per-route `authenticateToken` and the upstreams still authenticate, so the expected effect is a `5xx` or an upstream `401` where the canonical path gets the gateway's clean `401` or `405`, on the mixed public/authed mounts the gate exists for. Also check whether `resolveSpecRoute`'s regex matches case-insensitively.
2. **The brute-force login guard**, `middleware/security.ts:150`: `req.path.includes('/auth/login')` is case sensitive, so `/API/AUTH/LOGIN` never gets the helper attached. **Today this has no effect**: KS-1372 records that nothing in production calls `recordFailure`, so the lockout never engages on any spelling. The fold belongs in whichever fix KS-1372 takes (wire it or retire it), so it is listed here to be done once.
3. **The version prefix**, `index.ts:520` (the version parse), `index.ts:544` (the `/api/v1/` rewrite) and `routes/versioning.ts:48`: `/api/V1/...` and `/API/V1/...` are not recognised as the `v1` alias and answer `404`. That fails closed. Decide whether the alias should be case insensitive (parity) or left; either way pin it.
4. **CSRF exclusions match any prefix** (pre-existing; the KS-801 fold extends it to case variants equally): `csrf.ts` uses `startsWith(entry)` with no segment boundary, so `/api/auth/loginx` and `/api/verification/verifyX` are excluded from CSRF (measured by the gate on base and head). The `/api/verification/verify` entry deliberately covers `/verify-file` and `/verify-batch` by prefix, so the fix is to list those paths and match an exact path or a `/`-bounded sub-path, with a cell for each.

## Linked, not re-filed

* `audit.ts:210-212` (an upper-case `/API/` prefix is not audited): **KS-1191**, a design decision for the audit trail's owner.
* Path-scoped limiters and the spellings that dodge them: **KS-946**.
* The failed-login lockout being inert: **KS-1372**.
* The v1 verify family refused for cookie-bearing callers in production (the versioning redirect runs after CSRF): **KS-1177**.

## Also from the gate (nits, fixed in the PR for this ticket)

`ks801-path-fold.test.ts:20` says percent escapes are untouched, but the fold lowercases hex digits (`%4A` becomes `%4a`; harmless because no entry contains `%`); and the comment at `index.ts:396` runs two remarks together on one line.

## Detail

* **Source:** the Opus gate on PR #1459, 2026-10-12, defects 1 to 4 (`WEDNESDAY/0_Brain/reference/2026-10-12_gate-pr1459/verdict.md`), and Wednesday's instruction to file this first after the merge.
* **Searched first** (Linear, includeArchived, literal title/description matches): `bruteForceProtection` 2 (KS-1372, KS-1362), `security.ts:150` 0, `versioning.ts` 1 (KS-1177), `loginx` 0, `pathFold` 0, `case sensitive` 2 (KS-801, KS-861). None covers items 1, 3 or 4; item 2 is KS-1372's subject.

Related: KS-801, KS-1372, KS-1191, KS-946, KS-1177.

title: v1 verify family refused for cookie-bearing callers in production (versioning redirect runs after CSRF) while v2 passes
description:
## BLUF

In `NODE_ENV=production`, a cookie-bearing browser caller that sends no `X-XSRF-TOKEN` gets through on the v2 verify family but is refused on v1. The v1 call is redirected 307 to `/api/v1/verification/verify` by `versioning.ts`, which is production-only and mounted AFTER CSRF. The re-POST then meets `403 CSRF_TOKEN_MISSING`, because `/api/v1/` is not in `excludedPaths`. Pre-existing on the v1 side. PR #1001 (part of KS-1165) exempted v2, which turned "both refused" into "different" in production.

## Recommendation

Owner decision on the intended behaviour, then one of these:

* exempt the v1 verify family under its `/api/v1/verification/verify` spelling too;
* run the versioning redirect before CSRF;
* publish the difference in the spec if it is intended.

Pin the choice with a production-import cell (`NODE_ENV=production`).

## Detail

Found by the tier-1 QA gate on PR #1001 (KS-1165) at `3925d4c072b940eb91de462b7b92eabfe8889c75`, 2026-09-16. Report: `Testing Agent MAIN/projects/secuura/reports/2026-09-16-ks1165-1001-3925d4c07-tier1-r1/report.md`, section 7, F-2. The measurement, verbatim:

**F-2 — In NODE_ENV=production the v1 and v2 verify families diverge for cookie-bearing, header-less callers**

* Evidence class: MEASURED AT RUNTIME on a TRUE production import, replicated twice, plus the base-csrf run.
* Severity: **Minor**.
* Target: **TICKET** (pre-existing v1 routing/exemption interplay), noted against **KS-1165 DoD box 1**.
* SHIPS-WITH.
* Oracle: **P**roduct consistency (`csrf.ts:90-97` says the v1 verify family is exempt, but in production the redirected path is not). Also the PR title's claim "as v1's are", and box 1's "or the difference is published in the spec" (it is not).
* At head in production, cookie + allowed Origin + no X-XSRF-TOKEN:
  * `POST /api/v2/verification/verify` → **200** upstream (PT-1).
  * `POST /api/verification/verify` → **307 Location** `/api/v1/verification/verify` (PT-5; `versioning.ts:45-58` is production-only and mounted at `index.ts:530`, AFTER CSRF).
  * The re-POST the browser makes → **403** `CSRF_TOKEN_MISSING` (PT-6; `/api/v1/` is not in `excludedPaths`, as in M17).
* Controls:
  * PT-7: the same v1 alias with no cookie → 200.
  * PH-6 (hybrid): a valid double-submit token → 200.
  * Development PH-1: v1 → 200 with no redirect.
* At base in production, **both** families refuse this caller (v2 403: PT-1 red at base-csrf; v1 307→403 unchanged). So #1001 turns "same (both refused)" into "different" in production. Outside production they are the same at head (M1 = M3 = 200).
* Likelihood (READ ONLY; no browser):
  * The verifier portal calls `${VITE_API_URL || '/api'}/verification/verify` via `safeFetch`, which sends `credentials:'include'`, echoes `X-XSRF-TOKEN` when `document.cookie` holds it, and retries once on 403.
  * A same-site portal therefore probably passes on v1.
  * The refused shape is a cookie-holding caller that does not echo the header (cross-site cookie jar, or plain `fetch` with credentials), which is the caller class KS-1165 exists for, but on v1.
* Fix-shape (prose): exempt the v1 verify family under its `/api/v1/` spelling too, or run the versioning redirect before CSRF. The owner decides and publishes the difference if it is intended.

Not measured (report section 10): v1 `verify-file` in production (the 307 → alias path for octet-stream). F-2 is stated for `/verify` only.

Relation: KS-1165 DoD box 1 ("the v1 / v2 verify families behave the same for cookie-bearing callers, or the difference is published in the spec") is PARTIAL because of this. KS-1165's remaining close depends on this ticket existing plus its F-1 follow-up PR.

Dedupe before filing (seat A, 2026-09-16): literal matches over Linear `searchIssues` (archived and comments included), title + description + comments:

* `versioning.ts`: 0 of 117 results;
* `CSRF_TOKEN_MISSING`: 11 of 90 (KS-1165, KS-119, KS-188, KS-35, KS-428, KS-430, KS-46, KS-781, KS-798, KS-799, KS-841), none about the production versioning redirect running after CSRF;
* `/api/v1/verification`: 0 of 95;
* "versioning redirect": 0 of 113.
  Filed new.

title: api-gateway per-key limiter follow-up (KS-1195 gates): a JWT claim can name a key's bucket; refused requests still audited and validated; next() inside the try; unpinned guards
description:
## BLUF

The follow-up to KS-1195 (PR #1017, merged as `d7e95cd9f`). The per-key limiter now fires and buckets by the key, but the two tier-1 gates on #1017 left seven items open. None is reachable by a real producer today by READ, and none is a Major. In order of weight:

* **N-2:** a signed JWT can draw down a real key's allowance, by naming that key's bucket in a `rateLimitBucket` claim or an `api_key:`-prefixed `connectorId` claim.
* **F-5:** a refused mutation still writes an audit row, and a refused key still costs a validate (and, once the bearer cache expires, a token exchange).
* **F-4:** `next()` sits inside the limiter's `try`, so a synchronous throw downstream is counted twice and dispatched twice.
* **F-3 + N-1:** five guards no test cell can see.
* **R-2:** an unthrottled warn line per request.
* **The fallback literal:** `connectorId || userId` is still shared across tenants for JWT and test-token machine principals.

## Recommendation

Build as one tier-1 PR in the api-gateway limiter (`middleware/auth.ts` + `middleware/rateLimitEnforce.ts`), after KS-1195's live sweep. N-2 and the fallback share one fix; F-4 and F-5 are ordering changes in the same function; F-3 and N-1 are test cells only. No decision needed from anyone to start; the one product question (below) is recorded, not blocking.

## Detail

**Source:** the tier-1 gates on PR #1017. Round 1 `Testing Agent MAIN/projects/secuura/reports/2026-09-17-ks1195-1017-cbe29597d-tier1-r1/report.md` (F-3, F-4, F-5, R-2); round 2 `…/2026-09-17-ks1195-1017r2-a067d4e3e-tier1-r2/report.md` (N-1, N-2, the fallback Record, F-5 re-measured). Line numbers re-read at develop `d7e95cd9f153e9036ed77935a73c93504fa6e3dc`.

### N-2 (Minor, defence in depth): a JWT claim can name a key's bucket

* `rateLimitEnforce.ts:112` buckets by `user.rateLimitBucket || user.connectorId || user.userId`. The API-key branch sets `rateLimitBucket` (`auth.ts:300`), but the JWT branch copies the decoded payload into `req.user`, so a signed `rateLimitBucket` claim is honoured too.
* **Measured at round 2's head:** a victim key with limit 4 reads Remaining 3; an RS256 JWT with `authMethod api_key` and `rateLimitBucket = api_key:<the victim's bucket>` reads Remaining 2; the victim's next request reads 1.
* A signed `connectorId: api_key:<the victim's bucket>` does the same through the fallback (victim 2 → JWT 1 → victim 0). The gate's tamper that deletes the claim closes the first route and not this one.
* Controls: a test token carrying the claim keeps its own bucket (`parseTestToken` drops it); a JWT with `authMethod email` is not limited. Round 1 counted the same JWT in its own bucket, so honouring the claim is new with #1017.
* **Reach (READ):** needs the RS256 signing key. The auth signers emit `authMethod: 'oauth'` only; the connector-token mint carries no `authMethod`, `connectorId` or `rateLimit`. The bucket id is visible to log readers (the DEGRADED warn prints it).
* **Fix shape (the gate's):** honour `rateLimitBucket` only when the API-key branch set it (a WeakMap or non-enumerable tag on the request, not a `req.user` field), AND namespace the fallback (e.g. `jwt:${connectorId || userId}`), so no JWT claim reaches the `api_key:` namespace. No cell pins the claim either way today.

### The fallback literal (Record)

`connectorId || userId` is still the bucket for JWT and test-token machine principals, so two such principals in two tenants with the same connectorId or userId share one bucket (the F-1 class). No real producer reaches it by READ. N-2's namespacing fixes it.

### F-5 (Record): refused requests still cost audit rows and upstream calls

* Round 1, two keys under one connector, limit 1: A's refused POST answers 429 with 0 validates and 0 forwards, but **1 audit row** (`status 429`, `success false`, its own tenant). B's first POST (uncached) answered 429 **after validate 1 + exchange 1**.
* Round 2 re-measured with a new shape (the per-key bucket means B no longer starts refused): a refused request at **+61 s** (validate cache expired, bearer cached) costs **validate 1**, exchange 0, audit 1; at **+481 s** (both caches expired) **validate 1 + exchange 1**, audit 1.
* A flood of refused mutations is therefore a flood of fire-and-forget audit INSERTs and security-service calls. Attribution stays with the refused key's own tenant (no bleed).

### F-4 (Record): `next()` inside the limiter's `try`

* A synchronous throw from the continuation is caught by the limiter's own `catch`, counted a second time and dispatched a second time (probed: `nextCalls 2`, Remaining 5 → 3 → 1 in memory; with Redis, the throw is also logged as `redis-command-failed`, mislabelling a downstream error as a Redis failure).
* On the JWT branch the throw now escapes as an unhandled rejection (the client hangs). With production's default `UNHANDLED_REJECTION_MODE=exit` that path calls `gracefulShutdown` (READ, `index.ts`).
* **Unreachable today by READ:** 0 manual `authenticateToken(...)(...)` invocations; Express 4's `Layer.handle_request` catches handler throws.
* **Fix shape:** decide inside the `try`, call `next()` after it.

### F-3 + N-1 (Minor): guards no cell can see

Each row is a tamper the whole api-gateway suite does not notice (0 reds), measured by the gates:

* **G-OAUTH:** `'oauth'` added to `MACHINE_AUTH_METHODS` (`rateLimitEnforce.ts:61`). The real OAuth signer emits `authMethod: 'oauth'`, so this is the one real non-machine token type whose exemption nothing pins. (Related, not the same: KS-1156 records that the machine set never meets the `oauth` label.)
* **G-UNKOPT:** an unknown `sk_` key on an optional-auth route is given a principal and counted (22 unauthenticated rows gained `X-RateLimit-Limit 100`).
* **G-JWTCATCH:** the JWT continuation awaited inside the JWT branch's `try` (turns the hang into a 401).
* **G-BUCKET-HASH:** the bucket built as undomained `sha256(key)`, equal to the security service's stored `key_hash` (the gate's probe found the stored form in 64 of 64 bucket keys).
* **G-BUCKET-RAW-2:** the bucket built from the raw key (the raw key in 64 Redis keys).
* The property the last two break ("never the raw key, never equal to key_hash") holds at head, measured with planted controls. **Cell to add:** capture the fake-Redis command keys for two keys; assert `ratelimit:api_key:<hex>` differs from `sha256(key)` and does not contain the key.

### R-2 (Record): the unthrottled warn

`rateLimitEnforce.ts:104` logs `machine caller … has no rateLimit` on every request of a machine principal without an allowance: 197 lines in the gate's probe, all from JWT and test-token principals. The API-key branch always carries `|| 100`, so no real producer reaches it today.

### Product question (recorded, not blocking)

Whether two keys of one connector should share a bucket. #1017 follows KS-164's wording ("a key configured at N/min lets N through"): per key.

### Search before filing

`searchIssues` (includeArchived, includeComments), literal case-insensitive matches only: `rateLimitBucket` 2 fuzzy / 1 literal (KS-1195) · `enforceClientRateLimit` 6 / 6 (KS-1195, KS-170, KS-164 archived; KS-1196, KS-1197, KS-1198 by mention) · `has no rateLimit` 124 / 1 (KS-1195) · `per-key rate limit` 107 / 5 (KS-1195, KS-164, KS-1176, PS-319, KS-480) · `rateLimitEnforce` 9 / 9 (nearest KS-1156, the machine-set label record) · `limiter` 96 / 50 (none about these items). None covers them. Related: KS-1195, KS-1156, KS-1198.

title: Akto scans are now paced to fit the platform's rate limit — test times went up; which way should we go?
description:
## BLUF

Kamil, when you have a moment: **we need your decision on how the platform's rate limit should treat our Akto scans.** To stop 429s being counted as passes, the scans are now slowed to 1,500 requests/min using Akto's own rate limit (systemTest only, no platform code changed). Coverage is honest, but **pre-merge went from 47 s to 19 m 28 s, and the security tier now takes about an hour.** Six options are below, most of them gateway-side, which is yours. Once we've agreed one, either of us can make the change. **Reducing test coverage is not an option.** Thank you.

+++ What was added, and what it costs (measured)

**The pacing** ([KS-1286](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-1286/akto-image-2222-2356-latest-paired-local-pair-verified-2026-09-28-and) branch; [KS-709](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-709/akto-reports-a-pass-for-a-test-that-executed-nothing-clean-0-not) for the false passes it fixes)

* Akto reads a per-account `globalRateLimit` from its Mongo once a minute. `systemTest/akto/tests/tierPacingSetup.ts` sets it per tier: **pr unthrottled; pre-merge and security at 1,500/min** (0.75 × the platform's 2,000/min, derived in `src/setup/aktoRateLimit.ts`), restored to unthrottled afterwards. `AKTO_GLOBAL_RATE_LIMIT=N` overrides it.
* Before any setup login, the harness also waits (≤61 s, probing `GET /api/auth/me`) for the 60-second window to have room, since back-to-back tiers were having their setup logins refused ([KS-1362](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-1362/back-to-back-tiers-setup-logins-land-in-the-platforms-spent-60-second)).

**Measured on slot 2 of the Mac, 2026-09-28, Akto 2.35.6**

| tier | unpaced | paced at 1,500/min |
| -- | -- | -- |
| pr | 29 s — 8,702 results, 129 refused | (left unpaced) |
| pre-merge | **47 s** — only 1,057 actually tested, **8,129 refused** | **19 m 28 s** — 192 refused |
| full OWASP scan | 423.8 s — **8,730 of 50,162 refused** | **\~27 min — 0 of 50,306 refused** |
| whole security tier | — | **60 m 52 s** |

Two things to expect at any pace: Akto overshoots its setting by about 10%, and it releases each minute's allowance as a \~5 s burst, so the first minute of a paced run still sees a few refusals.

**The platform side as it stands** (read-only)

* Global limiter: `api-gateway/src/index.ts:472-485` — 60 s window, `max = RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS || (non-prod ? 10000 : 300)`; `.env.example:205` sets **2000**. Keyed per address, and every caller on the host shares `192.168.65.1` ([KS-618](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-618/client-ip-is-invisible-platform-wide-on-demo-every-ip-keyed-control)).
* Skip rules: `middleware/rateLimitSkip.ts` — read-only paths; an operator override `DISABLE_RATE_LIMIT=true` in non-prod envs; and a `Bearer test_token_` bypass when `ENABLE_TEST_TOKENS=true` in `development`/`test`.
* nginx (`nginx-demo.conf:171-172`, VM demo) adds `limit_req` at 50 r/s (api) and 5 r/s (auth).

+++

+++ The options, as I see them

1. **Keep things as they are** — harness-side pacing only; no platform change. *Cost:* pre-merge \~20 min and security \~1 h locally. The limiter stays exactly as deployed.
2. **Raise** `RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS` **for local stacks only** (e.g. back to the code's non-prod default of 10,000, or a figure you choose), leaving demo and production alone. The harness would pace to the new figure automatically, since it derives its rate from this value. *Cost:* local stacks stop matching the demo's limiter, so a limiter regression would be less likely to show locally.
3. **Use the existing operator override** — `DISABLE_RATE_LIMIT=true` on local non-prod stacks during scans. *Cost:* the global limiter is out of the picture entirely, including the verifier rate-limiting test's realism; easy to leave on by accident.
4. **Key the limiter per authenticated principal** (user or token) instead of per address — so the scanner's personas, k6 and a human each get their own budget. *Cost:* a real design change with security implications; overlaps [KS-618](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-618/client-ip-is-invisible-platform-wide-on-demo-every-ip-keyed-control).
5. **A dedicated, higher budget for a scanner identity in non-prod only** (e.g. a service account or a signed header, gated like the existing test-token bypass). *Cost:* a new bypass surface that has to be airtight to non-prod.
6. **Tune the harness further, no platform change** — pace closer to 2,000 (e.g. 0.85×) to save a few minutes at the price of a few more first-minute refusals, or pace fewer tiers. *Cost:* marginal gains; the limiter still sets the floor.

+++

## Where I'd love your guidance

1. Which option (or combination) fits how you want the limiter to behave?
2. Should local stacks match the demo's limits exactly, or is a looser local limit acceptable for testing?
3. Is \~20 min for pre-merge and \~1 h for security acceptable as a local gate, or is it worth a platform change to bring those down?

Once we've agreed a direction, either of us can make the change — whichever is more convenient. The one thing that isn't on the table is reducing test coverage: every option above keeps the same templates, tiers and endpoints, and changes only how fast they run or how the limit is set. No platform code has been touched so far.

## Checklist item added after the merge of PR #1347 (squash `8c810023f9c9`)

- [X] **N-1347-11 — the residue of the target-keyed pacing.** Closed by PR #1349, merged to `develop` as squash `691bb93e5c530c845ba0926ab0f369d5dc502720`: `isLocalScanTarget()` now reads `OVERRIDE_APP_URL` first and falls back to `SECUURA_API_URL`, the same precedence `systemTest/akto/src/scan/scanOptions.ts:98` uses for the host the scan attacks. With `RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS=10000` reaching the harness (a raised local `.env`), a scan aimed at a remote stack through `OVERRIDE_APP_URL` alone was paced at 7500/min and is now paced at 1500, and an `OVERRIDE_APP_URL` pointing at localhost is paced at 7500. Without that raised value, and without `AKTO_PLATFORM_REQUESTS_PER_MINUTE`, every target is paced at 1500, as before. Checked by unit tests only (9 cells: 4 that fail on the previous code, 5 controls); no Akto scan was run against any stack, and the demo's own `RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS` has not been read.

title: OAuth app registration accepts any scope list, and any authenticated user can register an app or change its scopes
description:
## BLUF

**Any authenticated user, whatever their role, can register an OAuth app, or change an app's scopes, with any scope list at all**, including the wildcard `*`, the privileged `subjects:erase`, and strings that are not scopes (`made:up`). Measured in-process on 2026-09-17 at develop `f8c7aaa39`:

* A plain `user` token gets **201** on `POST /api/oauth/apps` with `scopes ['*', 'subjects:erase', 'made:up']`, and those exact scopes reach `createApp`.
* The same token gets **200** on `PATCH /api/oauth/apps/:id` for an app id it was never given, and the new scopes reach `updateApp`.
* The gateway requires a token on these routes but checks no role before forwarding them to auth.

## Recommendation

Decide the shape before building. Three independent questions for the owner:

1. **Which scopes may an app be registered with?** A closed vocabulary (the canonical scope list rather than any string) would refuse `made:up` and `*` at the schema. Whether a caller may register a scope it does not itself hold, such as `subjects:erase`, is a separate rule.
2. **Who may manage OAuth apps?** Today it is anyone with a valid session.
3. **Does** `PATCH /apps/:id` **check that the caller owns the app?** The handler does not. Whether `updateApp` scopes the write by organisation or tenant was not read or measured.

## Detail

**Code at develop** `f8c7aaa39` (read):

* `services/auth/src/routes/oauth.ts:1148`: `oauthRouter.post('/apps', authenticate(), seedTenantGuc, …)`.
* `routes/oauth.ts:1245`: `oauthRouter.patch('/apps/:id', authenticate(), seedTenantGuc, …)`.
* Neither carries a role check. `requireRole` exists in `middleware/authenticate.ts:176` and is not used on these routes.
* `CreateOAuthAppSchema` (`:1132`, `scopes: z.array(pgSafeStringSchema).optional()`) and `UpdateOAuthAppSchema` (`:1237`, the same field) accept any NUL-free string.
* `authenticate()` (`middleware/authenticate.ts:121`) verifies an access token and a live session, and nothing else.
* The PATCH handler calls `updateApp(req.params.id, updates)` with no ownership comparison in the handler.
* The gateway mounts `/api/oauth` as a plain proxy to auth (`services/api-gateway/src/routes/proxy.ts:369`).

**Measured, auth side** (vitest, in-process). The REAL `oauthRouter` and the REAL `authenticate()` ran, plus `errorHandler`. Mocked: token verification (returns a `role: 'user'` payload), the session store (valid), `createApp` / `updateApp` (recording), the database, events and the logger.

* `CreateOAuthAppSchema.safeParse({…, scopes: ['*', 'subjects:erase', 'made:up']})` is true; `UpdateOAuthAppSchema` is true.
* `POST /api/oauth/apps` with no token: **401** `UNAUTHORIZED` "No token provided", `createApp` called 0 times (control).
* `POST /api/oauth/apps` as `role: 'user'`: **201**, response `allowedScopes ["*","subjects:erase","made:up"]`, `createApp` called once with exactly those scopes.
* `PATCH /api/oauth/apps/b0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000009` as `role: 'user'` with `scopes ['*', 'subjects:erase']`: **200**, `updateApp` called with `allowedScopes ["*","subjects:erase"]`. `updateApp` was mocked, so whether the real one would find or refuse another organisation's app is **not measured**.

**Measured, gateway side** (vitest, in-process, the REAL api-gateway app, `NODE_ENV=test`, auth and originate pointed at a recording server):

* `POST /api/oauth/apps` with no `Authorization`: **401** "Authentication required", **0** requests forwarded.
* `PATCH /api/oauth/apps/:id` with no `Authorization`: **401**, 0 forwarded.
* `POST /api/oauth/apps` with an RS256 access JWT for `role: 'user'`: **forwarded** (1 request `POST /api/oauth/apps` reached auth).
* Control: `GET /api/documents` with no `Authorization` is 401 with 0 forwarded.
* Caveat: in this harness the gateway's database is mocked (every query returns no rows), so this does not show how a revoked session is handled. It shows that no role gate refuses a valid `user` token.

**What a registered scope reaches (from Wednesday's defaults report, route-level, not re-run here):** with `allowedScopes ['subjects:erase']`, the authorize flow granted a code with scope `subjects:erase` (302). The code carries the grant into the token. Whether such a token then passes the erasure door as that user was **not measured** here. The KS-839 fix makes `*` grant nothing but does not affect a named privileged scope.

**Not measured:**

* live exposure (whether any registered app carries `*` or a privileged scope);
* whether the real `updateApp` is organisation-scoped;
* CSRF and the non-test gateway middleware order;
* the edge.

**Searched first** (Linear, literal matches in titles, descriptions and comments, archived included):

* `CreateOAuthAppSchema`: 3 hits (KS-821 and KS-824 on appType; KS-804 on authorize rules);
* `UpdateOAuthAppSchema`: 0;
* `/api/oauth/apps`: 19, none about who may register or which scopes;
* `POST /apps`: 2 (KS-821, KS-822);
* `register an OAuth app`: 0;
* `allowedScopes`: 5 (KS-839, KS-855, KS-804, KS-431, KS-822);
* `subjects:erase`: 7, none about registration.

**Source:** Wednesday's defaults report `/Volumes/DevMASTER/WEDNESDAY/2_Project_Files/local-model/night/briefs/DEFAULTS_2026-09-17_KS805-855-839.REPORT.md` (P8: the schema acceptance and the 302 grant), re-measured above with the role and gateway questions added.

title: The poller/reconcile blob writers also erase threadToken — on the CONFIRM/heal path, not just the failure path #936 fixes
description:
## BLUF

**The threadToken erasure KS-1058 fixed in** `markDocumentAnchorFailed` **is NOT the only writer that drops it. Every blob-rebuild writer in** `anchorStateSync.ts` **rebuilds** `blockchain: {...}` **as a literal with NO** `threadToken` **— including the CONFIRM and heal-to-confirmed paths.** So a document that mints a thread token at create and then anchors successfully has its `threadToken` cache erased on the success path, not just the failure path. Read from source, NOT runtime-measured.

## Mechanism (source, on develop `d4cf7e3cf`)

`updateDocument` replaces the `blockchain` column wholesale (`repositories/documentRepo.ts:480`, shallow top-level spread — established by KS-1058). Any writer that provides a fresh `blockchain` object therefore drops every field it does not re-list. The `anchorStateSync.ts` writers rebuild the blob from scratch with no `...existing` spread:

* `markDocumentAnchorFailed` **(:140)** — failure writer. **Fixed by #936 (KS-1058).**
* **poller confirm-writer (~:191)** — `blockchain: { txHash, blockHeight, anchoredAt, network, status, anchorId }` — no threadToken.
* **poller simulated-declaration writer (~:226)** — no threadToken.
* **reconcile heal-to-confirmed (~:299)** — `status: 'confirmed'` — no threadToken.
* **reconcile heal-to-simulated (~:327)** — no threadToken.

The confirm-writers are arguably the more serious of the set: they run on the **success** path, so a document that anchors normally loses the token cache that dashboards read (`state_thread_registry` is the canonical truth, but the whole point of the blob field per KS-1058 is to avoid that lookup).

## Why the type does not catch this

KS-1068 declared `threadToken?` as OPTIONAL (it is legitimately absent on many blobs), so a writer that omits it still compiles. The type makes the drop **visible to a reader**, not compile-fatal. Catching it needs either a spread-preserve pattern (as #936 applied to the failure writer) or a test per writer.

## Scope (behaviour — deliberately NOT KS-1068, which was type-only)

Decide, per writer, whether it should carry `threadToken` (and `simulatedTxRef`) forward — then either spread the prior blob or re-fetch the token from `state_thread_registry`. Same shape as KS-1058; extend that fix to the confirm/heal writers. **Verify at runtime first** — this ticket is a source read; a boot repro (mint → anchor → confirm, then read `document.blockchain.threadToken`) should confirm the erasure before the fix.

## Provenance

Surfaced by the KS-1068 writer re-check (scope item 3), 2026-09-10, read from source on develop `d4cf7e3cf`. Not runtime-measured. Sibling of KS-1058 (one instance fixed) and KS-1068 (the type hole).

title: Three new advisories freeze every push: in-range lock refresh for handlebars 4.7.9 -> 4.7.10
description:
## What is broken

Three `handlebars` advisories, published 2026-10-08T17:52Z, make the pre-push preflight refuse EVERY Secuura push on develop `1e7f90e26137`: leg 6 (npm-audit, KS-470) and leg 7 (standalone-lock advisories, KS-531). Trigger: Seat F 6th's KS-808 push was refused at 2026-10-08T23:26Z with `PREFLIGHT FAILED on leg(s) 6 7 - fix the above before pushing. (12/15 legs ran)`. Seat R 21st's #1427 merge-in push was refused the same way.

## Base control (Seat V 1st, 2026-10-08T23:45Z, clean scratch clone at develop 1e7f90e26137, 0 dirty locks asserted first)

* leg 6, `node scripts/audit/audit-gate.mjs`, rc 1: "FAIL — 3 NEW advisories not in the baseline": GHSA-xw65-4hp5-5hc7 \[moderate\], GHSA-8r5x-fm3f-whwj \[critical\], GHSA-p8wg-vrv2-v86f \[critical\].
* leg 7, `node scripts/audit/audit-locks.mjs`, rc 1: "FAIL — 3 advisories in standalone locks and NOT in the baseline", each `pinned: 4.7.9`, each `in 4 lock(s): services/governance, services/originate, services/referral, services/vc-issuer`.

## Census: 45 tracked locks, 5 handlebars entries in 5 locks

| Lock | Pinned | Flag | resolved / integrity | Parents (declared range) |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| Blockchain/Dev (workspace root, leg 6) | 4.7.9 | prod | no / no | ts-jest `^4.7.9`; member services/originate `^4.7.9` |
| services/governance | 4.7.9 | dev | yes / yes | ts-jest `^4.7.9` |
| services/originate | 4.7.9 | prod | yes / yes | root DIRECT `dependencies` `^4.7.9`; ts-jest `^4.7.9` |
| services/referral | 4.7.9 | dev | yes / yes | ts-jest `^4.7.9` |
| services/vc-issuer | 4.7.9 | dev | yes / yes | ts-jest `^4.7.9` |

## The fix: in-range, lock-only refresh 4.7.9 -> 4.7.10

* 4.7.10 clears all three. Leg 7's own instrument (the npm bulk advisory endpoint): 4.7.9 returns the three, each `>=4.0.0 <=4.7.9`; 4.7.10 returns `{}`. 4.7.10 is `latest` and the only release above 4.7.9.
* 0 of the 7 declaring parents refuse 4.7.10 (semver, with must-fail controls 5.0.0 and 4.7.8). So: no manifest edit, no `overrides`, no baseline row.
* The change is not version-only. 4.7.10 moves its own `dependencies.minimist` from `^1.2.5` to `^1.2.8`; every other lock-relevant field is equal. All five locks already resolve minimist at 1.2.8, so no other entry moves.
* Planned change set: 5 locks, 5 entries, 18 field writes, 0 manifests, 0 baseline, 0 source. Root entry: `version` + `dependencies.minimist` (it carries no resolved/integrity). Each standalone: `version`, `resolved`, `integrity`, `dependencies.minimist`.
* Integrity is taken from the downloaded 4.7.10 tarball (712,317 B); its sha512 equals the registry's `dist.integrity`. The same pipeline reproduces the 4.7.9 value the four locks carry today.

## Runtime reach

* services/originate: handlebars 4.7.9 IS in the runtime image. The runner re-installs from originate's own lock with `npm ci --ignore-scripts --omit=dev` (`services/originate/Dockerfile:79`), and handlebars is prod there.
* governance, referral: not at runtime. Both prune dev deps before the runtime copy (`npm prune --omit=dev`, `governance/Dockerfile:54`, `referral/Dockerfile:61`).
* vc-issuer: not at runtime. The runner installs `--omit=dev` from its own lock (`vc-issuer/Dockerfile:86`), where handlebars is dev.
* The Dev root workspace lock reaches no image (0 Dockerfile references; control: `package-lock.json` 8).
* 0 files in the repo import or require handlebars (controls on the same instrument: express 339, ts-jest 14). Present in one image; no code path found into it.

## Authority

Standing direction to BUMP rather than accept: Kam's cards `secuura-four-advisories-ruled-after-measurement` = bump (2026-09-09T10:30), `secuura-five-new-advisories-freeze-every-push-1006` = a, and `secuura-advisory-freeze-3-ghsa-1007` = a (G 3rd's round). No card exists for THIS freeze: 0 hits for `handlebars` in the decision store. This round rests on the standing direction plus Wednesday's ANSWER to F 6th. Ticket creation, one ticket per TEST PASS (Kam 2026-09-07 13:23): this is one pass, one ticket.

## Not done here

title: Security: four gateway path predicates are case-sensitive while Express routing is not — `/API/...` skips media-type enforcement on EVERY path, and is still proxied
description:
Filed out of KS-781's re-gate (3), finding **P3-5**. **Pre-existing** — not introduced by #812, and deliberately NOT fixed there (it is four predicates plus a routing-mode decision, which does not belong inside an OAuth security PR).

## Mechanism

`services/api-gateway/src/middleware/contentType.ts:91`:

```ts
if (!req.path.startsWith(ENFORCED_PREFIX)) return next();   // '/api/', case-sensitive
```

Express routing and the gateway's proxy mounts (`proxy.ts:317`, `router.use('/api/oauth', …)`) are case-**in**sensitive by default. So `/API/…` is **out of scope** to the guard and **in scope** to the router.

## Measured

```
G1 SCOPE TABLE (text/plain body — the class KS-439 exists to refuse)
  /api/oauth/apps      -> 415 refused
  /API/oauth/apps      -> PASSED THE CHOKE POINT
  /Api/oauth/apps      -> PASSED THE CHOKE POINT
  /api/auth/login      -> 415 refused
  /API/auth/login      -> PASSED THE CHOKE POINT
  /API/documents       -> PASSED THE CHOKE POINT

G2 PROXY MOUNT TABLE (real http-proxy-middleware, the real mount + rewrite)
  /API/oauth/authorize -> 200 {"sawPath":"/API/oauth/authorize","sawType":"application/x-www-form-urlencoded"}
```

The proxy forwards the upper-cased path unchanged, with the original content type.

## The class is four predicates, not one

Four security-relevant comparisons in the gateway are case-sensitive string tests over `req.path`, while everything that *routes* is case-insensitive:
`ENFORCED_PREFIX` · `FORM_ALLOWED_PATHS` · CSRF's `excludedPaths` · `proxyPaths`/`shouldParseBody`.
**Two fail closed** under case variation (CSRF's exclusions — CSRF applies where it was meant not to). **Two fail open.**

## ⚠ Bounded honestly

**The end-to-end consequence is NOT PROVEN.** Measured: the choke point is skipped, and the real proxy mount forwards the odd-cased path with its content type intact. **Not** measured: that a downstream service then *accepts* a mis-typed body — the target's own parser may still refuse it. Treat this as a **broken control**, not a demonstrated exploit, until someone drives it end to end.

## Fix shape

Either compare `req.path.toLowerCase()` in all four places, or `app.set('case sensitive routing', true)` so the router agrees with the string tests and an odd-cased path 404s. Prefer the second: it makes routing and every path predicate agree *by construction* rather than asking four call sites to remember `.toLowerCase()`.

## The regression test matters as much as the fix

The existing bound test (`api-gateway/src/__tests__/contentType.test.ts`) **fabricates** `req.path`, so it can only ever assert `Set.has()` — it cannot observe the enclosing scope check that decides whether the allow-set is consulted at all. That is why a case-sensitive scope test sat under a green suite. The replacement must drive the middleware over **real HTTP with real URLs** across a case/slash matrix, asserting refusal parity.

Source: QA re-gate (3) report, finding P3-5.
