**Give** `CLAUDE.md`**'s "rebuild local after any merge to** `develop`**" rule its own written exception**, so the next seat does not have to re-derive it — or, worse, skip it without measuring.

Current wording (project `CLAUDE.md`, "Local + new-Azure sync workflow" §1):

> *"After any merge to* `develop`*, rebuild local so it stays current."*

## Why

On 2026-09-09 (s161) #904 was merged to `develop`. Measured before spending ~30 min of image builds:

```
2 files:  systemTest/__tests__/pre_suite.test.sh            +26/-1
          systemTest/__tests__/quarantine_call_sites.test.sh +27/-1
files with a buildable/deployable surface: 0
```

No service, frontend, package, migration, Dockerfile or compose file. **An image rebuild could not have changed anything** — so the local `develop` ref was synced and the images left alone, and the report said so plainly rather than claiming "local rebuilt".

That was the right call, but it is the **second** time in one session a written rule needed a measured departure. **A rule with a legitimate exception that every seat rediscovers is a rule someone will eventually skip without measuring** — and the departure is invisible unless the operator volunteers it.

## Suggested wording

> *"After any merge to* `develop` *that touches a **buildable surface** (*`services/`*,* `frontend/`*,* `packages/`*,* `migrations/`*, a Dockerfile or a compose file), rebuild local so it stays current. A merge touching only test scripts, docs or CI config is a **measured no-op** — say so, name the file count, and sync the ref instead of rebuilding."*

The load-bearing half is **"say so"**: the exception is only safe while the operator states which branch they took and on what measurement.

## Scope note

⚠ **There are TWO copies of this file** — the project-root `CLAUDE.md` and the repo copy at `2_Project_Files/CLAUDE.md`. Both need the edit or they drift, which is its own recurring trap here.

## What is NOT established

Whether the rule has ever actually been skipped *without* a measurement. **Not swept** — this is filed on the near-miss shape, not on an observed incident.

Filed by s161 on Wednesday's instruction, 2026-09-09.

title: No independent liveness signal for our own VMs — kintsugi was dead for 53 h and Azure health read `Available` the whole time
description:
## BLUF

`secuura02-kintsugi-vm` **was down for 53 hours and nothing told us. The first signal was Stuart's tooling — a person, not a monitor. And Azure's own platform health read** `Available` **for the whole 53 hours, which is why the one alerting surface we do have would not have fired either.**

Both halves are one logical path — *we have no independent liveness signal for our own VMs* — so they are one ticket per Kam's 2026-09-06 aggregation rule, not two.

## What happened

* Azure live-migrated the VM at **2026-09-07T03:56:13Z** (`PlatformInitiated`, *"paused 0.993s, memory-preserving"*). The guest did not survive it.
* The workload died at ~**04:00Z**. On-disk logs **stop at 03:55:01Z** with **zero** entries for 53 h (control: **53** entries in the same hour).
* It came back only because a person went looking on **2026-09-09**, and was force-reset at **09:31:45Z**.

## Half 1 — no liveness signal

Nothing watches whether kintsugi is serving. There is no uptime check, no synthetic request, no alert on absence of logs. Detection was **incidental**.

⚠ This is the same shape as **KS-670** (demo's on-chain verification down **6 days**, found by a person). Two incidents, same missing control. That is the argument for fixing the class rather than the instance.

## Half 2 — the alerting surface we DO have was lying

Azure marked the box **Available at 03:59:30Z** and said *"no additional action is required"* — while the guest was dead and stayed dead for 53 hours. `memory-preserving` migration means **no reboot**, so Caddy survived in memory and kept answering at the edge while sshd, the guest agent and dockerd were all gone.

**So a health check that trusts either Azure resource health OR a naive port-200 on the front door would have reported green throughout.** Any monitor built here has to make a request that actually traverses the app, and has to alert on **silence** (no logs / no successful synthetic) rather than on an error, because a dead guest produces no errors at all — it produces nothing.

## Why this is due now

The incident record is closed (`5_Project_History/HANDOVER-kintsugi-outage-CLOSED.md`). **Recurrence is not** — Azure live-migrates this box as routine platform behaviour and the guest does not survive one. Boot diagnostics / serial console is now **ENABLED**, so a repeat leaves evidence; nothing currently tells us the repeat *happened*.

## Suggested shape (not a decision — the approach is open)

1. An external liveness check per VM (demo + kintsugi) that traverses the app, not just the edge — the front door answered while the box was dead.
2. Alert on **absence** — no successful synthetic in N minutes, or no new log lines — not on error responses.
3. Do **not** key anything off Azure resource health alone. This incident is the counter-example, in our own record.

## What is NOT established

* Whether the demo VM has the same exposure — **not measured**; it is the same subscription and region and probably does, but I did not check.
* The remount-read-only theory for the guest's death is **strongly supported, not proven**: no kernel message survived, because it could not be written to the disk it was about.

## Provenance

Azure activity log (read in slices — the API truncates silently at 50), the guest's own journal, `df` 37% and a clean `fsck` refuting ENOSPC and corruption from inside. Recorded by s160, filed by s161.

title: Connector erasure re-drive is unbounded against concurrency — and all three prescribed fixes are blocked (QA F-6)
description:
**BLUF — QA F-6. The connector erasure re-drive SELECT is unbounded against concurrency, and all THREE of the fixes prescribed for it are blocked by something measurable. Filing rather than half-building one, because each of the three fails in a way that is worse than the defect.**

The race (`services/originate/src/services/gdprService.ts`, `executeErasureByExternalRef`): the re-drive read

```sql
SELECT id FROM data_subject_requests
WHERE user_id = $1::uuid AND type = 'erasure'
  AND status NOT IN ('completed', 'denied')
ORDER BY requested_at ASC LIMIT 1
```

takes no lock. Platform S retries **without bound**, so two retries that overlap either both select the same DSR and both drive `executeErasureImpl` against it, or both miss and both file one — the orphan accumulation the re-drive was added to prevent.

### The three prescribed fixes, each measured

**1. Partial unique index — cannot be built on existing data.**

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … ON data_subject_requests (user_id)
  WHERE type = 'erasure' AND status NOT IN ('completed','denied');
```

Measured on the local database: **4 users already hold more than one non-terminal erasure DSR.** The index would fail to build. (Control: the same GROUP BY … HAVING count(*) > 1 without the type/status predicate returns **12**, so the query discriminates and the 4 is not a false zero.) This needs a data-reconciliation migration first — deciding which duplicate survives is a GDPR-records question, not an index.

**2.** `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` **— wrong for this shape.** If the row is locked by a concurrent attempt, SKIP LOCKED returns nothing, so the second caller falls through to the `else` branch and **files a new DSR**. That is precisely the accumulation the re-drive block exists to prevent, and the comment above it says so. Plain blocking `FOR UPDATE` is the right semantic, but it is inert outside an explicit transaction — a single `$queryRaw` commits immediately and drops the lock.

**3.** `prisma.$transaction` **+** `pg_advisory_xact_lock` **— deadlocks on the connection pool.** Transaction-scoped is the correct lock kind here (`pgbouncer.ini:54` is `pool_mode = transaction`, so a session-scoped advisory lock would leak onto whichever client next receives the server connection). But the block it would have to wrap calls `createDSR`, and `createDSR` issues its INSERT on the **module-level** `prisma` (`gdprService.ts:289`), not on the `tx` handle. So the inner write runs on a *different* connection, outside the transaction — losing the atomicity the lock was for — and worse, the outer transaction holds one pooled server connection while the inner call waits for another from the same pool. Under load that is a self-deadlock.

### What a real fix needs

Any of these, and each is its own piece of work:

* Thread a transaction client through `createDSR` (and `writePii`, which it awaits) so the claim and the INSERT share one connection — then the advisory lock works as intended; **or**
* an optimistic claim using the status vocabulary that already exists: a single atomic `UPDATE … SET status='processing' WHERE … AND status='pending' RETURNING id`, where losing the claim means another attempt is in flight. This needs a staleness timeout, or a crashed attempt strands the DSR in `processing` forever; **or**
* reconcile the 4 duplicate rows, then add the partial unique index and have the caller catch `23505` and re-read.

### Scope note

Not shipped in #790. That PR closes QA F-1 (denied DSRs re-driven) and F-5 (a test asserting its own fixture), both Majors, and adding a half-bounded lock would have made the concurrency story *look* handled while leaving the deadlock in. The re-drive block itself is not a regression from #790 — it was added in that PR's earlier revision and the unboundedness is inherent to the shape, not to the KS-695 change.

### Provenance

Measured 2026-09-02 (session 110) against branch `feature/ks-695-ask1-erasure-by-external-ref` at `b8d658d2a`, `develop` at `0e67228df`. Duplicate counts and the control read from the local Postgres read-only; `pool_mode` read from `docker/pgbouncer/pgbouncer.ini:54` and confirmed inside the running `secuura-pgbouncer` container. No writes.

title: Archiving a ticket silently archives its sub-issues, including NON-TERMINAL ones — and the parent-side check cannot detect it
description:
## BLUF

`issueArchive` **cascades to sub-issues.** Archiving 23 terminal tickets on 2026-09-08 also archived **KS-918 (Backlog)** and **KS-920 (In Progress)** — children of **KS-490**. Neither was in any target list. **In Progress is live work.**

**And the obvious verification cannot catch it:** once archived, the parent's `children` connection returns **nothing**. Asking the parent what it took with it reads clean.

Both were restored the same session. This ticket is about the mechanism, which is still live.

## Measured

```
child -> parent    KS-918.parent = KS-490      ✅ reveals the link
                   KS-920.parent = KS-490      ✅
parent -> children KS-490.children = 0         ❌ shows NOTHING
```

**The timestamps are what identified it as a cascade rather than a concurrent actor:**

```
KS-490  (mine, targeted)      archivedAt 2026-09-08T00:41:09.467Z
KS-921  (mine, targeted)      archivedAt 2026-09-08T00:41:09.467Z
KS-918  (NOT targeted)        archivedAt 2026-09-08T00:41:09.467Z   <- identical ms
KS-920  (NOT targeted)        archivedAt 2026-09-08T00:41:09.467Z   <- identical ms
```

Identical to the millisecond = one batch = one cause. **My own first diagnosis blamed a concurrent actor and was wrong; the timestamp disproved it.**

**Full accounting for the pass:** 33 intended + 2 collateral = 35 archived, measured 35. Only KS-490 had children, so the blast radius was bounded at exactly two.

## Why it went unnoticed until arithmetic caught it

The only reason anyone knows is the **census delta: −25 against an expected −23**. That is the shape most easily rationalised as a stale count. Every other signal looked clean:

* the archive calls all returned `success: true` — and they had, for the 23 asked;
* the parent-side `children` query returned **0**;
* no error, no warning, nothing in any response mentioning the children.

## The rule this produces

**Before archiving, query** `child → parent` **for the target's children and record the count. After, take a full paged census.**

```
expected delta = |targets| + |children found|
```

**If the delta is not exactly that, stop.** Asking the parent side for `children` is *the check that cannot fail* here — it reads zero both when there are none and when they have just been archived.

## Items

- [ ] **1. Make the children pre-check part of any archive procedure**, with the delta equation above as its pass condition.
- [ ] **2. Decide whether a cascade onto a NON-TERMINAL child should be refused outright.** Kam's standing ruling is that non-terminal work stays visible on the board; a cascade violates that silently.
- [ ] **3. Measure the historical population — see the sibling ticket** on the 95 pre-existing archived non-terminal tickets. This mechanism would produce exactly that.

Filed by s149, 2026-09-08, from the archive pass that hit it.

title: 95 archived tickets sit in NON-TERMINAL states — measure whether a cascade put them there
description:
## BLUF

**97 archived tickets on the KS+PS boards are in non-terminal states.** Two were archived today (mine, restored the same session). **The other 95 predate this session and nobody has established how they got there.**

```
Backlog     83
Todo         6
In Progress  4
In Review    3
Blocked      1
```

**This is a hypothesis with evidence, NOT an asserted cause.** [KS-995](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-995) established that `issueArchive` cascades onto sub-issues — including non-terminal ones — and that the parent-side check reads clean afterwards. **That mechanism would produce exactly this population, silently.** It may also be that some were archived deliberately.

## The measurement that would settle it

For each of the 95: **is its parent archived, and does the parent's** `archivedAt` **match the child's to the millisecond?**

That is the same discriminator that disproved a wrong third-party attribution during today's pass, applied backwards:

* **match → decisive for cascade.** One batch, one cause.
* **mismatch → closes nothing.** It was archived separately, which is consistent with a deliberate act.

One-directional, and that limit should be carried into whatever the measurement concludes — a mismatch is not evidence of intent.

## 🔴 Do NOT unarchive anything on the strength of this ticket

**83 tickets reappearing in Backlog changes what the team sees.** A restoration is as much a board change as an archive, and it is Kam's call on a measurement — not a tidy-up. **Measure first, report, then ask.**

## Items

- [ ] **1. Run the parent/timestamp measurement** across all 95 and report the split.
- [ ] **2. For any confirmed cascade victim, establish whether the work is still live** — an In Progress ticket archived by accident is different from a Backlog item nobody was going to do.
- [ ] **3. Only then** put a restoration proposal to Kam, with counts by state.

## Why it matters beyond tidiness

Every count taken with a default query has been wrong on this board today — *twice*. `Tested Not Deployed` read 24 when it was 29, and a Duplicate census read 4 when it was 5 because the query capped at 250. **If 95 live-state tickets are invisible, every "what is open" number anyone has quoted is short by some part of 95.**

Filed by s149, 2026-09-08, alongside KS-995.

title: The extranet test board has never shown a green run — 0 passed in 22, and the latest red is E2E 210/0 with Schemathesis producing no results
description:
## BLUF

**The team's own status board has never once been green.** The extranet Testing tab has recorded **22 Platform K runs since 2026-05-25: 17** `failed`**, 5** `error`**, 0** `passed`**.** Not one.

And the most recent red is misleading: **E2E passed 210/0**, and the run is marked failed because Schemathesis produced no parseable results.

A board that is permanently red is a board everyone learns to ignore — at which point it can never signal anything, which is the whole reason it was built ([KS-138](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-138), now Done and archived).

## Measured

`GET /api/tests/platform-k/runs` (22 runs, oldest 2026-05-25):

```
failed : 17
error  :  5
passed :  0
```

Latest dashboard (`GET /api/tests/platform-k/latest`, run of 2026-08-10T00:01:44Z, target "Azure Demo"):

```
✗ Findings to fix
  Schemathesis (API contract)   FAIL   — "No Schemathesis results parsed this run."
  End-to-end (e2e-v2)           PASS   — 210 pass · 0 fail · 10 skip · 2 flaky
```

So the one suite that produced results **passed cleanly**, and the red comes from the other leg producing nothing.

`platform-s` has **0 runs**, which is consistent and expected — [KS-139](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-139) (upload the S suite) is still open.

## A verdict bug in the generator, read rather than guessed

`secuura-extranet/ci/build-dashboard.mjs`:

```js
// :39
const schemathesis = (args.schemathesis || 'unknown').toLowerCase(); // success|failure|skipped|unknown

// :181
const schemathesisClean = smt.state === 'ok' ? realFail === 0 : schemathesis === 'success';
const overallPassed = schemathesisClean && e2e.ok;

// :190  — the BADGE, which handles 'skipped' correctly
pill(schemathesis === 'success', schemathesis === 'success' ? 'PASS'
     : schemathesis === 'skipped' ? 'SKIPPED' : 'FAIL');
```

**The badge and the verdict disagree about what** `skipped` **means.** Line 190 renders a skipped Schemathesis leg as `SKIPPED`; line 181 scores anything that is not exactly `'success'` as not-clean. The workflow passes `--schemathesis "${{ steps.schemathesis.outcome }}"`, and a skipped GitHub step reports `outcome: 'skipped'` — so **an e2e-only run is structurally incapable of reporting** `passed`, while its own dashboard says the missing leg was merely skipped.

Whether that is what happened on any given run I have **not** established — per-run dashboards return 404, so `latest` is the only one readable, and its badge says `FAIL` rather than `SKIPPED`, meaning that particular run's Schemathesis leg ran and failed rather than being skipped. **The verdict bug is real in the code either way**; it is not necessarily the cause of all 22 reds.

## Next action

1. **Fix the verdict/badge disagreement** — `skipped` should not fail a run, since the badge already says it does not. Small change, `build-dashboard.mjs:181`. *(Not done in this session: the extranet auto-deploys on push to* `main`*, and this session is under the deploy hold.)*
2. **Find out why Schemathesis produces no NDJSON** on the demo target — the artifact path is `systemTest/schemathesis/output/schemathesis-reports/schemathesis-output.ndjson`. This is the substantive half.
3. **Then** get one green run on the board, so a future red means something.

## The pattern

Fourth instance today of the same defect — **signals firing into channels nobody reads** — and the only one aimed at humans rather than CI:

* [KS-637](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-637) — nightly Internal Audit, 40 consecutive failures.
* [KS-636](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-636) — base-image watchdog flagged a CRITICAL, unread 13 days.
* [KS-635](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-635) — a baseline exception expiring 2026-08-31 whose owner is archived.
* [KS-634](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-634) — no gate runs the service unit suites.

This one is different in kind and worse in effect: the others are unread, **this one is read and disbelieved.**

*Found during the 2026-08-14 backlog sweep, running the extranet skill's test-runner review that boot skipped.*

title: APP_DB_PASSWORD is a committed literal :- default in docker-compose.yml — 51 sites, not the ~20 the register records
description:
## BLUF

`APP_DB_PASSWORD` **is committed as a literal** `:-` **default in** `Blockchain/Dev/docker-compose.yml` **— 51 times.** A fresh volume bakes it in, and it is the password behind ~20 service connection strings. Split out of [KS-490](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-490) (Review E, row E-1) so it can be fixed without dragging the whole review stream.

## Measured, not relayed

Against `develop` `541acae81` (2026-09-03):

```
literal  APP_DB_PASSWORD:-YuBz…  defaults : 51
control  any APP_DB_PASSWORD reference  : 53
```

So **51 of 53** references carry the committed literal. The value begins `YuBzECVdrAU9…` and is 32 characters.

**The Review E register understates this: it says "~20 connection strings".** The true figure is 51 sites. Recording that because a fixer sizing the change off the register would plan for a third of the work.

## Why it matters, stated precisely

It is a **local-dev** compose file, not production — that is the honest framing and it is why this is High and not Urgent. But:

* It is a real credential in a public-ish repo's history. Removing the default does not un-commit it; the value is in git history from whenever it landed, so the fix is **remove the default AND rotate**, not just remove.
* `:-` means the literal is the *fallback*, so any environment that has not set `APP_DB_PASSWORD` silently runs on the committed value. That includes a fresh clone, which is the common case for a new team member.
* The same file binds Postgres to `127.0.0.1` (E-4, now fixed), so the exposure is loopback — but a container on the same host is not on loopback-only terms with it.

## Done when

1. No literal `:-<secret>` default remains in `docker-compose.yml` — the variable is required, and the stack fails loudly if it is unset rather than falling back.
2. The value is rotated, and `Blockchain/Dev/env.example` documents the new variable.
3. **Stuart and Peter are told before it merges** — this is the one change here with a team cost: their local stacks will need `APP_DB_PASSWORD` set, and a stack that "fails loudly" will fail loudly for them first. That is a batched-notify item, not a surprise.

## Not done here, and why

I have not made this change tonight. It is a one-file edit, but requirement 3 makes it a coordination item rather than a quiet fix, and requirement 2 (rotation) touches a credential — @kam's call on both the timing and whether rotation is in scope for a local-dev password.

Filed from session 111 during the KS-490 ACTION-row pass. Searched first: no existing open ticket (`title contains "APP_DB_PASSWORD"` → 1, KS-8, **Done** and about a different defect in `01-create-app-role.sh`; `"committed credential"` → 0; `"compose password"` → 0; control `"password"` → 8, so the query discriminates).

title: KS-869's COALESCE backfill has an EMPTY window — the 39 pre-existing keys never backfill, so the KS-843 cutover flip still has no usable evidence
description:
## BLUF

**KS-869 does not fix the KS-843 cutover's evidence problem for keys that already exist.** The `COALESCE(EXCLUDED.connector_id, svc_api_keys.connector_id)` backfill I described as filling pre-fix rows "for free" **has no window in which to fire**. Found by the KS-869 tier-1 gate; **correcting my own claim** in that PR body.

## Why the window is empty

`connectorId` enters an `ApiKey` object in exactly two places:

* at **mint** (`services/security/src/index.ts:1004`), or
* from the **row** (`:345`, `rowToApiKey`)

`memApiKeys` is warmed **only from the database at boot** (`:376-381`). The deploy restarts the service, so every pre-fix row re-warms with `connectorId` **undefined**; every later save therefore passes NULL; and `COALESCE` correctly declines to overwrite with NULL. **"The next save backfills it for free" is true only for keys minted after this deploys.**

## The consequence, and it lands on KS-843

Kam's 2026-09-06 13:59 logged-grace ruling flips `SUBJECTS_ERASE_SCOPE_ENFORCED` **once the log shows Platform S on the new key**. After KS-869 merges and deploys, the `[KS-843]` grace log will **still record** `connectorId: null` **for every EXISTING Platform S key**. The flip's evidence is not restored by KS-869 alone.

## FIRST ITEM — the measurement that decides the fix

**Does anything on the row determine the connector?** Check `key_prefix`, `organization_id`, `name` (the mint sets `name` to `Platform S connector — <org|externalRef>`) against the 39 existing rows (measured 2026-09-06; this ticket originally said 43). If one of them does, a one-off backfill is possible. If none does, **the answer is a re-mint of Platform S's keys** — which is Stuart's window and therefore Kam's call, and it merges with the KS-577 rotation conversation rather than being a separate ask.

## Acceptance

Either the 43 rows carry a correct `connector_id` (backfilled from a source named in the measurement above), or a ruling is recorded that Platform S's keys will be re-minted, with the flip explicitly waiting on it. **KS-843's cutover comment must be updated either way** — today it says KS-869 is the prerequisite; if that is not sufficient, it should say so.

title: Every ADMITTED erasure authenticates twice — the door's chain and the catch-all both run authenticateToken, doubling a remote key validation on a partner path
description:
## BLUF

On the erasure path an **admitted** request authenticates **twice**; a refused one authenticates once. Measured fresh by the round-3 gate across 14 shapes × 2 modes: **refused = 1, admitted = 2**.

Carried out of KS-861 when #845 merged, per the ruling that F-11 is a follow-up and not a gate item. **Not a live defect — a cost defect on a partner-facing path.**

## Mechanism

`services/api-gateway/src/routes/proxy.ts`:

* `:677` — the erasure door's chain carries `authenticateToken(true)`
* `:696` — the catch-all `router.use('/api/gdpr', authenticateToken(true), proxy('originate', …))` carries it again

An admitted request passes through the door, `next()`s, and hits the catch-all's copy. A refused one is stopped by the responding handler, so the second never runs — the correct direction, and why this is a cost issue rather than a correctness one.

## Why it matters

In production `authenticateToken` validates an `sk_` key **over HTTP** to the security service — `services/api-gateway/src/middleware/auth.ts:257` → `validateApiKey:209` → `POST /api/keys/validate`. So every admitted erasure doubles a remote call on a partner-facing path. It surfaces as latency, not as an error, which is why nothing has flagged it.

## Fix shape (from the round-2 tester)

Either the door's chain omits `authenticateToken` and relies on the catch-all's, or `authenticateToken` short-circuits when `req.user` is already set. **The second touches shared auth middleware and therefore every route** — it wants its own measurement rather than being folded in as an obvious win.

## Note on the round-3 fix

The F-9 fix (an inner express `Router`) was checked against this and **does not** close it for free — that was the stated condition for folding it into round 3, and it was not met.

## Acceptance

An admitted erasure invokes `authenticateToken` **once**, driven by counting invocations of an injected factory (the harness in `ks843-erasure-path-bypass.test.ts` already injects one); a refused erasure still invokes it once; guardrail behaviour and the 403/200 outcomes across the 14 shapes are unchanged.

title: Merge protocol: the server-side `sha=` pin protects the PR head, not the base — a 9-second race merged onto an unapproved parent and invalidated the gate's predicted tree oid
description:
## BLUF

**The merge protocol we were running could not enforce its own central assertion.** "Sha-asserted against a tip re-read in the same minutes" was executed via `PUT /repos/{o}/{r}/pulls/{n}/merge -f sha=…` — and **that** `sha` **pins the pull request's HEAD. There is no base parameter on that endpoint.** So the base could move between the assertion and GitHub executing the merge, and the merge would silently succeed onto a parent nobody had approved.

Measured, not theorised. This ticket is the record for the next reader; the fix is already ruled and in force.

## What happened (PR #852, 2026-09-06)

| time | event |
| -- | -- |
| 04:27:09Z | asserted `develop` = `81bf7b078`, exactly as the GO named |
| 04:27:18Z | **#848 (the other seat) merged** → `606aa385b` |
| 04:27:20Z | #852 merged onto `606aa385b`, **not** `81bf7b078` |

A **nine-second** window, with the protocol followed exactly.

## What it cost

**Nothing in content.** #848 touched only `.githooks/pre-push`; #852 touched only four `deployment/azure` files; `git diff --name-only 81bf7b078 af078257` returns all five, so both landed and the sets are disjoint.

**Something in evidence.** The gate's predicted merge-tree oid `82acc2da…` was computed against `81bf7b078` and is **not** the tree that exists — the real tree is `39acb349…`. A reviewer checking the merge against the predicted oid finds a mismatch and is right to stop. That is the actual damage: a correct merge that cannot be checked against its own gate's prediction.

## The ruling now in force (both seats)

1. Merge from **your own checkout**: `git ls-remote origin develop` → `git fetch origin develop` → `git merge --no-ff --no-edit <pr-head-sha>` onto `origin/develop` as read → `git push origin HEAD:develop`.
2. **No** `--force`**, no** `--force-with-lease`**.** A plain push already refuses a non-fast-forward, so **a base that moved turns a silent wrong merge into a refused push** — which is exactly the property wanted. On refusal: re-read, re-merge onto the new tip, push again, and **the receipt names both attempts**.
3. **Every receipt carries the base line:** `first parent = <sha>` beside `asserted = <sha>`. Equal → "base held". Different → name what landed, whether the file sets are disjoint (measured with `diff --name-only`), and that the gate's predicted tree does not apply.
4. A gate's predicted merge-tree oid is carried as **"predicted against base** `<sha>`**"**. A differing first parent invalidates the **prediction**, not the merge — re-derive `merge-tree` against the real first parent and name the new oid.
5. The server-side `PUT … sha=` shape stays acceptable **only for a seat merging alone**, which with two parallel seats is never.
6. **Serialising the seats was explicitly not ruled** — parallel stays. The mechanism above is what makes a lost race safe.

## Why this is filed rather than just fixed

The mechanism is already in force from the next merge. What a ticket preserves is the *reason*: a future reader seeing `PUT … sha=` in old receipts, or wondering why we push a merge commit by ref instead of using the API, needs the nine-second timeline above — otherwise the API call looks simpler and someone reintroduces it.

## Acceptance

No further build. Closed when the merge shape above appears in `CONTRIBUTING.md` / `docs/DEV-PROCESS.md` alongside the existing merge-flow section, with the timeline as its justification.

title: Enable Code Security / GHAS so security scans populate the Security tab (currently artifact-only)
description:
## Source

Surfaced fixing [KS-237](<https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-237>) (repair Gitleaks + Semgrep on PRs). When the repaired Semgrep job first ran on a PR, `upload-sarif` failed with `Resource not accessible by integration` **(403)**. Root cause confirmed via the API:

```
GET /repos/Secuura/Distributed_Secuura  → security_and_analysis:
  code_security: disabled
  secret_scanning: disabled
  dependabot_security_updates: disabled
GET /repos/.../code-scanning/analyses    → 403 "Code Security must be enabled for this repository to use code scanning."
```

## Problem

**Code Security / GitHub Advanced Security is disabled on the repo**, so `github/codeql-action/upload-sarif` can't write to the **Security → Code scanning** tab. This affects **every SARIF-based scan**, not just Semgrep:

* Gitleaks ([KS-237](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-237/repair-gitleaks-semgrep-security-scan-actions-invalid-sha-pins-semgrep)) and Semgrep ([KS-237](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-237/repair-gitleaks-semgrep-security-scan-actions-invalid-sha-pins-semgrep))
* Container Security Scan (Trivy) — uploads SARIF
* the CodeQL upload steps

[KS-237](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-237/repair-gitleaks-semgrep-security-scan-actions-invalid-sha-pins-semgrep) worked around it: SARIF upload is now best-effort (`continue-on-error`) and findings are published as **workflow artifacts** (`gitleaks-sarif`, `semgrep-sarif`) so they're accessible. But the Security-tab integration (de-duped findings, PR annotations, dismissal workflow, trend view) is dark until GHAS is enabled.

## Decision needed (Kam / Peter)

GitHub Advanced Security is a **paid** add-on for private repos. Options:

1. **Enable GHAS / Code Security** — the upload-sarif paths light up with no further code change; findings land in the Security tab with PR annotations + dismissal workflow. Cost per active committer.
2. **Stay artifact-only** — keep the current best-effort uploads + artifacts; findings are in the run artifacts, no Security-tab UX. Free.
3. **Make the repo public** — GHAS/code-scanning is free for public repos (not in scope / a product decision of its own).

## Acceptance (if option 1 chosen)

- [ ] Code Security enabled on `Secuura/Distributed_Secuura`
- [ ] (optional) Secret scanning + push protection enabled — overlaps with the gitleaks job
- [ ] A PR's Semgrep/Gitleaks/Trivy SARIF appears under Security → Code scanning
- [ ] The `continue-on-error` on the SARIF-upload steps can then be removed (so a genuine upload failure is visible again)

## Related

* [KS-237](<https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-237>) — the workaround (artifact fallback) lives here
* [KS-230](<https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-230>) — wired the scanners onto PRs
* [KS-231](<https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-231>) — Dependabot activation (same "security feature not actually on" class)
* [KS-229](<https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-229>) — assurance tracker

title: KMS: move platform wallet mnemonic to Key Vault (KS-326 follow-up)
description:
**Follow-up carved out of** [KS-326](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-326/phase-0-crypto-agility-foundation-kms)**.** [KS-326](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-326/phase-0-crypto-agility-foundation-kms) (Phase 0 — crypto-agility + KMS) was closed as Done, but only the **JWT signing key** half of its KMS item actually shipped (PR #361/#362 — JWT private key now loads from Azure Key Vault with an env fallback). The **platform wallet mnemonic** was left behind and is still loaded from an env var.

**Current state (verified in code):**

* `PLATFORM_WALLET_MNEMONIC` is read from `process.env` in `services/anchoring` (e.g. `services/anchoring/src/index.ts:850`), then passed to `initWallet(mnemonic, network)` in `services/anchoring/src/cardano/wallet.ts` to derive the BIP-39 → BIP-32 → Ed25519 signing key.
* The JWT-key KMS plumbing already exists to reuse: `packages/shared/src/vault/key-vault.ts` (Key Vault `getSecret` with env fallback).

**Ask:**

- [ ] Load `PLATFORM_WALLET_MNEMONIC` from Azure Key Vault via the existing `key-vault.ts` helper, with an always-on env fallback (mirror the JWT-key pattern, so local/dev with no Key Vault still works).
- [ ] Support rotation (versioned secret) — note a mnemonic rotation also rotates the derived wallet address, so document the operational impact.
- [ ] Keep behaviour-preserving defaults: no Key Vault configured → falls back to `PLATFORM_WALLET_MNEMONIC` env, identical to today.

**Why it matters:** the mnemonic is the platform wallet's root secret; leaving it in env is a wider blast radius than the JWT key that already moved. Not urgent (env is the current accepted posture), but it closes the gap [KS-326](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-326/phase-0-crypto-agility-foundation-kms) implied was done.

**Refs:** [KS-326](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-326/phase-0-crypto-agility-foundation-kms) (parent, closed), PR #361/#362 (JWT-key KMS pattern to follow), `docs/security/POST-QUANTUM-CRYPTO-MIGRATION-PLAN.md` §5 Phase 0 / §7.

title: Wire the status-page XSS probe into preflight (or decide not to) — it runs today only by hand
description:
## BLUF

`scripts/security/status-page-xss-probe.mjs` exists, passes, and is **proven able to fail** — but nothing runs it automatically. Decide whether it joins `scripts/preflight/preflight.sh` as a 7th check.

## Recommendation

Wire it in, in a session scoped to preflight. Not as a rider on a security PR.

## Why it was left unwired

`frontend/status/index.html` is a static page with no `package.json` and no test runner, so the probe has no suite to live in. Preflight is the natural home — it is explicitly "the cheap cross-cutting sweeps the per-package gates miss", and this is exactly that shape.

But preflight is the **shared pre-push gate**. Adding a check to it changes the pre-push path for Peter and Stuart, and a new gate that turns out to be flaky blocks their pushes in a repo where neither knows a change happened. That is the reasoning Wednesday set on KS-628 and it applies unchanged here: being permitted and being right are different questions.

## What wiring it involves

* Add a 7th step to `scripts/preflight/preflight.sh` invoking `node scripts/security/status-page-xss-probe.mjs` from `Blockchain/Dev`.
* The probe needs no running stack and no network — it reads the file and drives the page's own `render()` in-process, so it is fast and deterministic.
* Its one fragility: it parses the page's `<script>` block by string split. If the page gains a second `<script>` or moves to a bundler, the probe exits 2 with an explicit "page structure changed" message rather than passing silently. Worth confirming that failure mode is acceptable in a gate before adding it.

Filed from session 30 alongside the KS-487 B-5 fix.

title: node:24-alpine carries a CRITICAL (CVE-2026-59873) — our own base-image watchdog flagged it on 2026-08-01 and the failure went unread
description:
## BLUF

**The base-image CVE watchdog fired on 2026-08-01 and nobody heard it.** Its scheduled run failed — which is, by the workflow's own design, the alarm — reporting `node:24-alpine`**: 1 CRITICAL / 4 HIGH — CVE-2026-59873**. That is the base image for **all ten backend services**.

Thirteen days unread at the time of filing. The watch is monthly, so without intervention the next signal is **2026-09-01**.

## Evidence

`.github/workflows/base-image-refresh.yml`, run `30685775724`, `event=schedule`, `created 2026-08-01T05:24:40Z`, `conclusion=failure`. Failing step: **"Evaluate watch conditions"**. Job log:

```
=== Trivy scan (CRITICAL/HIGH) of fresh local bases ===
  node:24-alpine                            : 1 CRITICAL / 4 HIGH — criticals: CVE-2026-59873
  nginx:1.30-alpine                         : 0 CRITICAL / 0 HIGH
  nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.30-alpine   : 0 CRITICAL / 0 HIGH
  edoburu/pgbouncer:v1.25.2-p0              : 0 CRITICAL / 2 HIGH
  redis:8-alpine                            : 0 CRITICAL / 0 HIGH
  postgres:15-alpine                        : 1 CRITICAL / 14 HIGH — criticals: CVE-2025-68121
```

The postgres critical is the known [KS-365](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-365) residual (local-dev surface only, upstream's to fix) and is **not** why the run failed. The run failed on **Case 2** of its own contract:

> The run FAILS in exactly two cases, both worth a human: … 2. any OTHER base reports a CRITICAL → a pinned base has re-accumulated a critical CVE; treat like KS-363 (refresh/bump + redeploy).

`node:24-alpine` is that other base. The workflow did exactly what it was built to do.

**Every pinned base also reported** `MOVED` — all six tags were republished upstream since the last pull, so the images we build on are behind their own tags regardless of the CVE.

## Scope

`node:24-alpine` is the `FROM` for **10 service Dockerfiles** (`nginx:1.30-alpine` for the other 2). So this is not one service — it is the whole backend, local and demo alike.

## What I have NOT established

* **Whether CVE-2026-59873 is exploitable in our usage.** I did not look it up: the project rule forbids fetching external URLs/changelogs unless asked. Someone should read the advisory before sizing this.
* **Whether it is still present today.** The scan is from 2026-08-01 and the tag has moved since. It may already be fixed upstream — a re-run answers it in minutes.

**Neither gap is a reason to leave it.** A critical on the base image of every service, flagged by our own watchdog and unread for a fortnight, is worth a human either way.

## Next action

1. **Re-run the watch now** (`workflow_dispatch` on `base-image-refresh.yml`) to get a current reading rather than a fortnight-old one.
2. Read CVE-2026-59873 and decide: rebuild on the moved tag, bump the base, or accept with a written reason.
3. If a rebuild is needed it lands behind the Kintsugi hold like everything else — it is a rebuild of every service image.

## The process defect, which is the more important half

**A failed scheduled run is this watch's ONLY notification channel**, and it is one nobody checks. The workflow header says so plainly: *"Scheduled-run failures notify via GitHub, which is the reminder."* That reminder went nowhere for 13 days.

Same shape as [KS-635](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-635) (an audit-baseline expiry whose owning ticket was archived) and [KS-634](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-634) (no gate runs the service unit suites): **we have signals that fire correctly into channels nobody reads.** Worth deciding once, for all three, where an unattended failure should actually land.

*Found during the 2026-08-14 backlog sweep while verifying KS-365.*

title: Frontend CSP quality: issuer alone carries 'unsafe-eval', and all three portals allow 'unsafe-inline' styles
description:
## BLUF

**The three portals each ship their own Content-Security-Policy, and that placement is correct — but two of the policies contain directives that materially weaken them.** Spun out of [KS-491](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-491)'s F-9 row so that row can close on what it actually claimed (no CSP at the edge — false), without losing the real question it surfaced.

**This is a quality review of the existing policies, NOT a request to add a gateway CSP.** The gateway deliberately does not own CSP (`docker/nginx-gateway/nginx-demo.conf:240-245`, added in `045c658ec`), and adding one there would compose by intersection with these and break the portals. See KS-491's close banner for that evidence.

## What is served today — measured at the live demo edge, 2026-08-17

Read-only GETs against `https://secuura02-demo.southeastasia.cloudapp.azure.com`:

| Portal | Path | Notable directives |
| -- | -- | -- |
| Issuer | `/` | `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval' 'unsafe-eval'`; `frame-ancestors 'none'` |
| Admin | `/admin/` | `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'`; `frame-ancestors 'self'` |
| Verifier | `/verify/` | `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'`; `frame-ancestors 'self' https://*.secuura.io https://secuura.io` |

All three additionally carry `style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://fonts.googleapis.com` and `style-src-attr 'unsafe-inline'`.

Source: `frontend/issuer/nginx.conf`, `frontend/verifier/nginx.conf`, `frontend/admin/nginx.conf` (issuer/verifier build theirs from `${csp_*}` variables); `frontend/outlook-addin/nginx.conf` has its own, and is **not** routed through this gateway.

## The two weakenings

1. `'unsafe-eval'` **on the issuer portal only.** The other two run on `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` alone, which is the narrower grant and evidently sufficient for them. Worth establishing whether the issuer still needs full `eval`, or whether this is residue — if it is residue, removing it is the single highest-value change here.
2. `'unsafe-inline'` **on** `style-src` **/** `style-src-attr`**, all three portals.** Common in Vite/React builds and not trivially removable (it usually needs nonces or hashes threaded through the build), but it is the directive most often cited in a customer security questionnaire.

## Recommended shape

* Establish whether the issuer's `'unsafe-eval'` is load-bearing. If not, drop it — one-line change, verify the portal still renders and signs.
* Cost the `style-src` nonce/hash work separately before committing to it; it is a build-pipeline change, not a config change.
* **Do not** consolidate these into a single shared policy. The differences between them are real (Blockfrost origins for issuer/verifier, `wss://` for admin, three different `frame-ancestors`), which is precisely why the gateway abstains.

## Not urgent

No exploit is claimed here. `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'self'`, `form-action 'self'` and explicit `frame-ancestors` are all already present on every portal, so the policies are well-formed; this is about tightening two directives, not repairing a gap.

title: [Decision] @secuura/shared is imported by 24 services and declared by 2 — the symlink pattern is invisible to every lockfile and audit gate
description:
## BLUF

**24 services import** `@secuura/shared`**. Only 2 declare it. The other 22 resolve it because a Dockerfile creates a symlink — which means the dependency is invisible to** `npm ls`**, to** `npm audit`**, to the lockfile gates, and to anyone reading a** `package.json` **to learn what a service depends on.**

Spun out of [KS-647](https://linear.app/secuura/issue/KS-647) so that ticket can close on its actual scope (flipping mcp-server + vc-issuer to `npm ci`, which needs none of this). **This ticket is the design decision underneath it.**

## The measurement — `develop 2129cdc8b`, 2026-08-17

|  | Count | Detail |
| -- | -- | -- |
| Services importing `@secuura/shared` in source | **25** | incl. `services/shared` itself |
| Service Dockerfiles creating `ln -s /shared node_modules/@secuura/shared` | **24** | the resolution mechanism |
| Services **declaring** it in `package.json` | **2** | `mcp-server`, `vc-issuer` — both as `"*"` |
| Services importing it with **no declaration** | **22** | analytics, anchoring, api-gateway, auth, billing, demo-service, governance, guardian, kyc, m365-integration, nft-certificate, originate, prism, queue, referral, security, staking, tenant-provisioning, timestamping, tokenisation, transfer, wallet-connector |

The root `package.json` declares `workspaces: ["packages/*","services/*","frontend/*"]`, so this resolves cleanly at dev time via the workspace hoist. **The Docker build does not use the workspace root** — each service builds from its own context with its own `package.json` and standalone lockfile — so the symlink is what makes it work in an image.

## Why this is worth a ticket rather than a shrug

It works today, and the pattern is deliberate and consistent. The cost is in what it hides:

1. **Audit blindness.** `@secuura/shared` and anything it depends on appear in no service lockfile. The KS-470 audit gate and the KS-531 standalone-lock audit both read manifests and lockfiles — neither can see this edge. A vulnerability reachable only through `@secuura/shared` would be invisible to both gates.
2. **No version pinning.** Nothing records which version of the shared package a service was built against. `packages/shared` is at `0.3.0`; no consumer references that, so a breaking change in the shared package is discoverable only by rebuilding and booting each service.
3. **It is not self-describing.** Reading `services/auth/package.json` does not tell you the service depends on `@secuura/shared`. Twenty-two services are in that position.
4. **The two exceptions prove it is confusing.** `mcp-server` and `vc-issuer` declared the dependency — the intuitively correct thing — and that is precisely why they cannot use `npm ci`, and why they carry `sed -i` lines to undo their own manifests.

## Options (not a recommendation — this is the decision to take)

**A. Formalise the workspace.** Declare `"@secuura/shared": "workspace:*"` and build service images from the workspace root rather than per-service contexts. Correct and self-describing; the cost is a change to every service Dockerfile's build context and probably the CI image-build matrix.

**B. Publish** `packages/shared` **to a private registry** (GitHub Packages on the existing org). Every service declares a real version, locks resolve normally, audit tooling sees the tree. The cost is a publish step in CI and a registry credential in every build.

**C. Keep the symlink, make it visible.** Leave the mechanism alone but add `@secuura/shared` to a documented allowlist that the audit tooling explicitly accounts for, so the blind spot is recorded rather than accidental. Cheapest; does not fix pinning.

**D. Do nothing, deliberately.** Defensible while the shared package is small and changes with its consumers. Should then be written down as a decision, because right now it reads as an accident.

## Acceptance

A decision recorded with its reasoning, and — whichever option — the audit blind spot either closed or explicitly documented in `scripts/audit/`, so a future reader does not assume the lockfile gates cover this edge when they do not.

## Not urgent

No known vulnerability rides on this today. Filed so the design question stops being rediscovered every time someone touches a Dockerfile — it has now surfaced through KS-374, KS-384 and KS-647.

title: KS-78 drift check is wrong three ways — reports 7 commits of drift where 212 exist, labels `develop` as `main`, and anchors to a stock redis image
description:
## BLUF

**The KS-78 local-drift check reports a number that is real but labelled with the wrong branch, anchored to the wrong containers, and computed from the wrong kind of timestamp.** Today it printed **7 commits** of drift. The drift that actually exists, measured against the oldest code image in the running stack, is **212**.

Three independent defects, all in `Launch_Claude.command:465-481`. Diagnosed 2026-08-17 (session 43) after **two consecutive sessions (41, 42) flagged the warning as unreconcilable and moved on** — s42 recorded it in project history as an open question handed forward. That is the cost: *two sessions discounted a TRUE warning because its label pointed at a branch that had not moved.*

## Defect 1 — the label says `main`; the code measures `HEAD`

```sh
# Launch_Claude.command:475
DRIFT_COUNT="$(git -C "$GIT_REPO_DIR" log --oneline --since="$EARLIEST_START" 2>/dev/null | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
# Launch_Claude.command:476-477
printf '[KS-78 drift warning] %s commit(s) on main since the running stack was built (%s).\n' "$DRIFT_COUNT" "$EARLIEST_START"
```

`git log` is invoked with **no revision argument**, so it walks `HEAD` — the currently checked-out branch. The word `main` is hardcoded in the `printf` and has never been measured.

**Discriminating control**, all against the same baseline instant `2026-08-17T00:52:38.647560758Z`:

| what was run | count |
| -- | -- |
| `git log --oneline --since=<S>` (exactly what the launcher runs) | **7** |
| `git log --oneline --since=<S> develop` | **7** |
| `git log --oneline --since=<S> main` | **0** |
| `git log --oneline --since=<S> origin/main` | **0** |
| `git symbolic-ref --short HEAD` | `develop` |

The no-rev form agrees with `develop` and disagrees with `main` — that is the discriminator, not an inference.

**Why it was ever right:** KS-78 closed **2026-05-15**, when `main` *was* the working branch. Git Flow (KS-137) made `develop` the integration line on **2026-05-25** — ten days later. The check never measured `main`; it measured `HEAD`, which happened to be `main` on the day it shipped and silently became `develop` a fortnight after.

## Defect 2 — `StartedAt` is restart time, not build time

`EARLIEST_START` comes from `docker inspect --format '{{.State.StartedAt}}'`. That is when the container process **last started**, which moves on any `docker start` / `restart` / `compose up` **without any rebuild**.

Proven on the live stack rather than asserted — `secuura-redis`:

```
Created    : 2026-08-12T21:42:23Z
StartedAt  : 2026-08-17T00:52:38Z   <-- 4 days later
RestartCount: 0
```

The container was not rebuilt and not auto-restarted, yet its baseline moved forward four days.

**The practical false negative:** `docker compose down && docker compose up -d` (no `build`) sets every `StartedAt` to *now*, so `DRIFT_COUNT` becomes **0** while every image on disk stays exactly as stale as it was. The check goes silent in precisely the situation it exists to catch.

## Defect 3 — the baseline is anchored to containers that hold no repo code

`EARLIEST_START` is the **minimum** `StartedAt` **across every** `secuura-*` **container**, and that set includes stock upstream infrastructure images. Today the anchor is `secuura-redis` → `redis:8-alpine`, **image built 2026-06-22**; the oldest image of any kind in the stack is `postgres:15-alpine`, **built 2026-02-26**. Neither contains a line of this repo.

Meanwhile the oldest **code** image actually running is `secuura-website-frontend`, built **2026-07-19T00:15:56Z**.

**Measured consequence:**

| baseline used | commits on `develop` since |
| -- | -- |
| what the check used (earliest `StartedAt`, from a stock redis) | **7** — what it printed |
| oldest **code** image build time (`website-frontend`, 2026-07-19) | **212** |

**The check understates real drift by roughly 30x.** It answers "how long since you last ran `compose up`", not "how stale is the code you are running".

## Suggested fix (not applied — see below)

Compute the baseline from **image build time of code-bearing containers only**, and name the branch it actually measured:

```sh
BRANCH="$(git -C "$GIT_REPO_DIR" symbolic-ref --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo HEAD)"
# oldest .Image .Created across containers whose image is locally built (not a registry tag)
DRIFT_COUNT="$(git -C "$GIT_REPO_DIR" log --oneline --since="$OLDEST_IMAGE_BUILT" "$BRANCH" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
printf '[KS-78 drift warning] %s commit(s) on %s since the oldest running image was BUILT (%s).\n' "$DRIFT_COUNT" "$BRANCH" "$OLDEST_IMAGE_BUILT"
```

Filtering "code-bearing" is the one judgement call: `.Config.Image` for locally built services is `2_project_files-<svc>` (no registry host, no upstream tag), whereas infra is `redis:8-alpine` / `postgres:15-alpine`. That distinction is available without extra tooling.

## What I deliberately did NOT do

**No edit to** `Launch_Claude.command`**.** It is boot-path infrastructure for every session, it is **not under version control** (project root is not a git repo — git lives at `2_Project_Files/`), and there are **16 copies of the template across the workspace**, so a fix here fixes one of sixteen. Changing it is Kam's call, and Wednesday is carrying the fleet-wide fix on the WED board gated on his go-ahead, citing this ticket as the evidence.

## Acceptance

1. The warning names the branch it actually measured (or measures the branch it names).
2. The baseline is image **build** time, not container **start** time — verified by a negative control: `compose up -d` with no rebuild must **not** reduce the count.
3. Infra containers built from upstream tags do not set the baseline — verified by a positive control: the reported count matches the count computed from the oldest locally-built image.

title: Security events carry no tenant at all — KS-743 had to gate them platform-only, which is a workaround for the data model
description:
## BLUF

**Security events are authorised platform-only because they carry no tenant — not because platform-only is the right long-term answer.** KS-743 gated `GET /api/events` and `PATCH /api/events/:id/resolve` to platform roles. That is the only authorisation that is *true* of the surface today, and it is a workaround for a data-model gap.

## The gap, measured

* `SecurityEvent` (`services/security/src/index.ts:95-107`) has **no tenant field**: `id, eventType, severity, source, userId?, ipAddress?, details, resolved, resolvedAt?, resolvedBy?, createdAt`.
* `svc_security_events` (`migrations/002_verification-tiers.sql:536`) has **no tenant column**.
* `dbSaveSecurityEvent` (`index.ts:181`) INSERTs **eleven** columns — `id, event_type, severity, source, user_id, ip_address, details, resolved, resolved_at, resolved_by, created_at`. None is a tenant or an organisation.

So there is no `targetTenantId` to hand `decideTenantAccess`, which is exactly why the read could return the whole cross-tenant corpus to an ordinary tenant admin (measured before the fix on the local published gateway: **200,** `total: 651`).

## Consequence of the interim gate

A tenant admin can no longer see security events **for their own tenant either** — because there is no such thing as "their own" yet. That is a real capability loss, accepted deliberately over leaking every tenant's events. It is also invisible today: a sweep of `frontend/` found **zero** references to `/api/security/events` (control: **3** for `/api/security/audit`, which the admin dashboard does use), so nothing in the product currently asks for it.

## What the fix would involve

1. `tenant_id` on `svc_security_events` + a migration, with a decision on what to backfill existing rows to — they have no recoverable tenant, so a NULL/`unknown` sentinel and a policy for reading those.
2. `tenantId` on `SecurityEvent`, derived from the verified JWT at `POST /api/events` (the same server-derived shape `POST /api/audit` already uses at `index.ts:556-561`, deliberately never from the body).
3. Swap `requirePlatformOperator` for `decideTenantAccess` on the two read/write routes, keeping platform cross-tenant reach.
4. Producers: every internal caller of `POST /api/events` needs to be carrying a tenant-bearing token, or the sentinel path has to be defined for them. **Not enumerated here** — that sweep is part of the work, not of this description.

## Status of this description

Points 1-3 are a **design sketch, not an agreed plan**. Point 4 in particular is unmeasured. Whether events should be tenant-scoped at all, rather than remaining a platform-operations surface with a proper operator console, is the actual product question and is **open** — this ticket exists so that question is asked deliberately rather than inherited from a gate I added under time pressure.

Follow-up to KS-743 (PR #778). Filed session 100.

title: svc_api_keys.organization_id is not a tenancy boundary and nothing keeps it coherent with tenant_id — an incoherent pair is storable
description:
## BLUF

`svc_api_keys.organization_id` **is not a tenancy boundary and nothing keeps it coherent with** `tenant_id`**.** An incoherent pair — an org belonging to tenant B stored against `tenant_id` = tenant A — **is storable**, and RLS then resolves the row entirely in favour of `tenant_id`, because the policy never consults `organization_id`.

**Not a live escalation.** Post-KS-742 the application enforces tenancy on both `GET` and `POST /api/keys`, and DB-layer isolation is working as designed (measured below). This is an **integrity gap**: future code that treats `organization_id` as implying a tenant would be wrong, and nothing in the schema would stop it.

Raised by Peter on the KS-742 thread ("the org/tenant pair can be made incoherent … bounded, and unmeasured by me"). This is the measurement.

## Measured on LOCAL

**Constraints — read, not inherited. **`svc_api_keys` has exactly **one** constraint:

```
svc_api_keys_pkey | p
```

No foreign keys, no check constraint tying `organization_id` to `tenant_id`. `018_svc_api_keys_reconcile.sql` was read in full: it does ADD COLUMN, a backfill (`organization_id` → `organizations.tenant_id`), NOT NULL, an index and RLS — and **adds no constraint of any kind**. The backfill sets the pair coherently *once*; nothing holds it that way afterwards.

**Storability — proven, nothing persisted.** An INSERT of `{organization_id: <an org owned by tenant fd4254fd…>, tenant_id: a0000000-…-0001}` was **accepted** (`INSERT 0 1`) inside a transaction that then **ROLLED BACK**. Post-rollback control: rows matching the probe id = **0**. I used a rollback rather than a persisted write because it answers the same question and leaves no credential behind.

**What the GUC then shows.** The `tenant_isolation` policy keys on `tenant_id` alone:

```
(current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true) IS NOT NULL
 AND current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true) <> ''
 AND tenant_id::text = current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true))
OR current_setting('app.tenant_scope_bypass', true) = 'platform_admin'
```

So an incoherent row is visible to **tenant A's** admins (its `tenant_id`) and invisible to **tenant B's** (its org's real owner). `organization_id` plays no part.

## ⚠ Two corrections to my own reading, recorded because they nearly became findings

**1. A** `qual=true` **policy that looked like a hole is not one. **`svc_api_keys` carries a second policy, `svc_api_keys_auth_lookup`, PERMISSIVE / SELECT / `qual=true`. Permissive policies are OR'd, so at first read that appeared to defeat tenant isolation for every reader. **It does not** — it is scoped to `roles={secuura_auth_lookup}`, a dedicated role, while `tenant_isolation` applies to `{public}`. Same pattern on `users` and `oauth_apps`. It is a correctly-scoped carve-out for the credential-lookup path, which must find a key by hash *before* a tenant context exists. **Recording it positively so nobody "fixes" it later.**

**2. My first RLS measurement was worthless.** I connected as `secuura` — `super=true bypassrls=true` — so RLS never applied and every count came back unfiltered. The control that caught it: `documents` (a single fail-closed policy, no auth-lookup policy) returned the same 95,015 with and without a dead tenant GUC, which is impossible if the GUC were filtering.

**Re-measured as** `secuura_app` (`super=false bypassrls=false`), with controls that fire in both directions:

| session | rows |
| -- | -- |
| no GUC | **0** |
| GUC = a nonexistent tenant | **0** |
| GUC = the default tenant | **480** |
| `app.tenant_scope_bypass = platform_admin` | **1165** |
| as `secuura_auth_lookup`, no GUC | **1165** (its policy, as intended) |

So the fail-closed policy is genuinely fail-closed for the runtime role, and the instrument can return non-zero — the 0s mean something.

## Fix shape (not done here)

Either a `FOREIGN KEY (organization_id) REFERENCES organizations(id)` plus a trigger or check asserting `tenant_id` matches that org's tenant, **or** an explicit decision that `organization_id` is descriptive metadata and never a boundary — written down where the next reader will find it. The second is cheaper and may be the right answer; what should not persist is the current state, where the field *looks* like a boundary and is not.

⚠ Adding an FK is not free: `organization_id` is NULL-able by design (018 §2, so the originate admin path can issue tenant-scoped keys with no org), and the s99 record notes demo held a synthetic org with no `organizations` row. Any FK needs that data cleaned first.

Filed session 100, KS-742 follow-up 6(b). No fix this session by instruction.

title: The GitHub integration walks Linear tickets on branch names and PR bodies — 4 unrequested state changes in one night, all reverted by hand
description:
## BLUF

**The GitHub↔Linear integration moves tickets nobody asked it to move, and the board has been silently wrong between each walk and the next manual revert.** Four measured walks in one night, on three different tickets, all with `actor = automation`. Every one had to be reverted by hand, and one ticket was walked twice.

## Measured (2026-09-02, all times UTC)

| time | ticket | walk | trigger |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| ~13:1x | KS-229 | `Backlog → In Review` | #789's body cites KS-229 |
| 14:32 | KS-365 | `Tested Not Deployed → In Progress` | #793 opened |
| 14:33 | KS-365 | `In Progress → In Review` | #793 opened |
| 14:44 | KS-229 | `Backlog → In Review` | #785 pushed; branch `docs/ks-229-encryptedfield-header` |

The trigger is an identifier appearing in a **branch name or PR body**. That is not a statement about the ticket's state, and the integration treats it as one.

## Why it is worse than cosmetic

* **A tracker ticket walked to In Review implies its whole finding set is with a reviewer.** KS-229 is the 2026-06-10 assurance-review tracker; #785 closes one Low finding under it. The board said the tracker was in review; it was not.
* **It walks tickets OUT of terminal states.** KS-365 was walked off `Tested Not Deployed`, which is part of a census Kam asked to keep visible. A state Kam is reading as a count can be changed by opening an unrelated follow-up PR.
* **It can move someone else's ticket.** An identifier in a branch name transitions that ticket regardless of who owns it — already recorded as a known trap on this board.
* The walks are only ever caught because a human or agent happens to be watching the history API. Between the walk and the revert, the board is wrong and nobody is told.

## Done when

1. The integration's state mapping is either **disabled** for automatic transitions, or narrowed to a signal that actually means something (a merged PR that *closes* the ticket via a `Closes #`-style link, not a branch-name substring).
2. A stated rule for what an automated transition is allowed to do, written where the board rules live.
3. Until (1), the standing practice is recorded: **any automated transition on a tracker ticket is noise — walk it back with a one-line comment naming the PR.**

## Notes

Filed from session 111 after the second KS-229 revert of the night. Not urgent — it is board hygiene, not a platform defect — but it is a recurring manual tax and it makes the board unreliable as a record precisely when several PRs are moving at once.

Searched before filing: no existing ticket covers this (`title contains "auto-transition"` → 0, `"walk"` → 1 unrelated, `"integration"` → 12 all unrelated; control `"erasure"` → 3, so the query discriminates).

title: Merge helper must refuse a non-read SHA and have no fallback that re-derives its own expectation — the #774 gate could not fail
description:
## BLUF

**A merge gate that asserts the head SHA can be made unable to fail, and it was, tonight, on PR #774.** Two defects combined; the second is the dangerous one and it is mechanically preventable.

## What happened (s112, 2026-09-03)

The merge helper takes an *expected* head SHA and refuses to PUT if the PR's actual head differs.

1. **The expected SHA was fabricated.** It was produced by extending a 9-character prefix (`21ba93b49`, copied from a boot report table) into a full 40-character string — 31 invented hex characters. `git cat-file -t` on it returns *"fatal: could not get object info"*; on the real head, `commit`. It was never a repo object. This is the second instance of the standing line *"a SHA is READ or it is not used — never extended from a prefix"* in two sessions.
2. **The recovery deleted the assertion.** The call was written as:

   ```
   merge_helper 774 <fabricated> || merge_helper 774 "$(gh api …/pulls/774 --jq .head.sha)"
   ```

   The fallback **re-reads the head from the API and passes it back as the EXPECTED value**, so `expected == actual` by construction. That gate cannot fail. #774 was merged behind a head-check that proved nothing.

The merge itself was correct — the reviews check is an independent gate, ran against the real head, and the PUT carried that same read SHA — but one gate of six was self-confirming and nothing in the tooling said so.

## The standing line this produced

> **A fallback that re-reads the value it is asserting has deleted the assertion — a retry may change the ACTION but never the EXPECTATION.**

Adopted fleet-wide. This ticket is the mechanical half, in this repo.

## Done means

A committed merge helper (`scripts/` — replacing the ad-hoc per-session one) that:

1. **Refuses an expected SHA that is not exactly 40 hex characters.** A prefix is a hard error with a message naming the rule, not a silent widening.
2. **Reads the expected SHA itself**, in the same invocation, from `git ls-remote refs/pull/<n>/head` or the pulls API — and takes the *comparison* value from a second, independent read, so the two can disagree.
3. **Has no fallback path that re-derives the expectation.** A STOP is terminal. A retry may re-read the *actual*, never the *expected*.
4. **Verifies the approval independently** — `commit_id == head.sha` on `/pulls/{n}/reviews` — and requires `mergeable_state == clean`, so no single gate carries the decision alone.
5. Ships with a **self-test** proving each refusal fires: a short SHA rejected, a mismatched SHA rejected, a stale approval rejected, and a valid case allowed. The self-test is the control — a gate whose refusals are never exercised is a gate nobody knows works.

## Why it is worth committing rather than remembering

Every session so far has re-written this helper inline, which is why the same class recurs. The rule is cheap to encode and expensive to re-learn: the last two sessions each lost a round to a SHA that was not read.

title: Decide the 17 baseline entries that carry no `expires` — permanent acceptance, or dated exception?
description:
## BLUF

**17 of the 35 baseline entries carry no** `expires`**, and each one is a decision nobody has made explicitly.** They predate the expiry requirement and read as permanent acceptances — unreachable code paths, build-tree-only dependencies — which is why they were written without a date. Since KS-763 they are enumerated in `GRANDFATHERED_NO_EXPIRY` (`scripts/audit/baseline-contract.mjs`) rather than admitted by a missing-field check, so the set is now **countable and closed**: any *new* entry without `expires` fails the gate. This ticket is the decision on the 17 themselves.

## The ask

For each entry: does it stay a permanent acceptance, or does it become a dated exception with a review date? A permanent acceptance is a legitimate answer — it just has to be an answer, rather than a field nobody filled in.

## The set

Predicate: every key in `accepted` with no `expires`, at `develop` `e02e15811`. Count re-derived, not copied.

| GHSA | package | deciding ticket |
| -- | -- | -- |
| GHSA-2mjp-6q6p-2qxm | undici | KS-470 |
| GHSA-35p6-xmwp-9g52 | undici | KS-470 |
| GHSA-4992-7rv2-5pvq | undici | KS-470 |
| GHSA-5qjj-4xww-7phc | valibot | KS-493 |
| GHSA-848j-6mx2-7j84 | elliptic | KS-470 |
| GHSA-8xcm-r25x-g524 | undici | KS-559 |
| GHSA-92pp-h63x-v22m | @hono/node-server | KS-470 |
| GHSA-g8m3-5g58-fq7m | undici | KS-470 |
| GHSA-g9mf-h72j-4rw9 | undici | KS-470 |
| GHSA-m8rv-5g2x-5cg5 | undici | KS-559 |
| GHSA-p88m-4jfj-68fv | undici | KS-470 |
| GHSA-v2v4-37r5-5v8g | ip-address | KS-470 |
| GHSA-v3r7-h72x-cjcm | undici | KS-559 |
| GHSA-v9p9-hfj2-hcw8 | undici | KS-470 |
| GHSA-vrm6-8vpv-qv8q | undici | KS-470 |
| GHSA-vxpw-j846-p89q | undici | KS-470 |
| GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq | uuid | KS-470 |

**13 of the 17 are** `undici`, all resting on the same acceptance (the issuer build tree; no backend service pulls it), re-verified 2026-08-12 against all 27 backend standalone locks. If that reasoning still holds, those 13 are one decision, not thirteen.

## Why it matters

The baseline's own `$comment` says entries with `expires` are temporary exceptions pending a fix — which implies entries *without* one are permanent. Nothing in the file states that, and until KS-763 nothing enforced it either. Someone reading a bare entry cannot tell "we decided this is permanently fine" from "we forgot the date".

## Done when

Each of the 17 either (a) carries an `expires` and leaves `GRANDFATHERED_NO_EXPIRY`, or (b) carries an explicit note in its `reason` saying it is a permanent acceptance and why re-review is not needed. The set shrinks to what was consciously chosen.

## Not in scope

Changing any acceptance. Nothing here says the 17 are wrong — only that their permanence is currently implicit.

Filed from session 113. The enforcement half shipped on `feature/ks-763-audit-gate-validate-fields` `6c6d94d94`.

title: audit-locks scans 35 of 45 lockfiles — 3 vulnerable locks have coverage from neither gate
description:
## BLUF

`audit-locks.mjs` **scans 35 of the repo's 45 lockfiles, and three of the ten it cannot see carry a vulnerable package right now** — with coverage from neither gate. The script prints "35 standalone lockfiles" as its headline, which reads like a total; it is a *surface*, and the surface is ten locks short of the repo.

## Measured

`findStandaloneLocks()` (`Blockchain/Dev/scripts/audit/audit-locks.mjs:77-88`) is hardcoded to:

```js
for (const top of ['services', 'packages', 'frontend', 'scripts']) {
```

— one level deep, four top-level directories, all under `Blockchain/Dev`. Everything else is invisible to it.

Locks outside the scan, at `develop` `e02e15811` (all 45 locks parsed from the git blobs):

| lock | vulnerable content | covered by anything? |
| -- | -- | -- |
| `Blockchain/Dev/connectors/whatsapp-bot` | **qs@6.14.2** | **NO** — `connectors/` is simply not in the list |
| `systemTest/akto` | **fast-uri@3.1.5** | **NO** — repo root, outside `devRoot` entirely |
| `systemTest/api-explorer` | **fast-uri@3.1.5** | **NO** — same |
| `Blockchain/Dev/package-lock.json` | fast-uri@3.1.5, qs@6.15.3 | yes — audit-gate's hoisted root scan |
| `Blockchain/Dev/mobile/secuura-app` | — | no |
| `Blockchain/Dev/tests/e2e`, `tests/e2e-v2` | — | no |
| `observability` | — | no |
| `systemTest/performance`, `systemTest/playwright` | — | no |

`qs@6.14.2` is inside both GHSA-4mjr-xmp4-gh2g and GHSA-x5fp-wj9c-mxmx. `fast-uri@3.1.5` is inside all four of the HIGH fast-uri advisories (GHSA-5jgf / GHSA-f65p / GHSA-fph4 / GHSA-jqff — SSRF and host confusion).

## The consequence that has already bitten us

**#794's fast-uri baseline row says the advisory is present in FIVE locks. It is present in SEVEN.** The row was written from what the gate can see, and the gate cannot see `systemTest/akto` or `systemTest/api-explorer`. Applying that five-file list as a fix set would have left two locks on `fast-uri@3.1.5`, kept the advisory live, and made a correct fix look like it had failed.

The same blind spot means `connectors/whatsapp-bot`'s `qs@6.14.2` has never appeared in any gate output, in either direction — it is not baselined and not reported.

## The ask

Widen the discovery so the gate's count is the repo's count, or state the exclusions deliberately. Both are defensible; what is not defensible is a hardcoded four-directory list that silently decides the scope. Two shapes worth considering:

1. **Discover, don't enumerate** — walk for `package-lock.json` from the repo root, excluding `node_modules`, and let an explicit deny-list carry any genuine exclusions with a reason each.
2. **Keep the list, print the gap** — if `systemTest/` and `connectors/` are deliberately out of scope, the script should say so in its output and name what it skipped, so "35 lockfiles" is never read as "all of them".

`lockfile-cleanroom.sh` has the same four-directory shape (`find services packages frontend scripts`) and would need the same treatment to stay consistent.

## Done when

Every `package-lock.json` in the repo is either scanned, or excluded by a named rule with a recorded reason; and the script's summary line states its surface rather than implying a total. `connectors/whatsapp-bot`'s qs and the two `systemTest` fast-uri pins are triaged either way.

## Not in scope

Fixing the three vulnerable locks. The `fast-uri` overrides for `systemTest/akto` and `systemTest/api-explorer` are already applied on `feature/ks-763-fast-uri-overrides` `7b40543a3` (KS-763); `connectors/whatsapp-bot`'s qs is blocked by tilde parents like the other 27 (see KS-763's measurement comment).

Filed from session 113 — found while red-proving the KS-763 gate hardening: the gate's own scan output disagreed with my lockfile parse, and the gate was the one that was short.

title: S revokes that emit no lifecycle event, or emit share-permission-change, are indistinguishable on K from a document that was never revoked
description:
## BLUF

**K cannot tell a revoked document from one that was never revoked, when S's revoke path emits no lifecycle event — and cannot tell a revoke from an ordinary permission change when S emits** `share-permission-change` **instead of** `share-revoke`**.** Both are silent on the K side. Raised from Stuart's PS-749 split (PS-764/765/766/767) as the **K-side** question those S-side findings imply; no S-side work is proposed here.

Measured read-only on `develop`, 2026-09-04. Nothing was written.

## The two cases, and what K actually sees

| S behaviour | K row | Can K distinguish it from "never revoked"? |
| -- | -- | -- |
| emits `share-revoke` | `action='share-revoke'` | **Yes** — this is the working path |
| emits `share-permission-change` (two Edit-dropdown paths) | `action='share-permission-change'` + free-form payload | **No** — not without parsing a payload K does not own |
| emits nothing (Outlook add-in revoke, PS-765; and the Share Now **reuse path **`:402-420`, which applies permission and expiry changes and records neither) | **no row at all** | **No — identical by construction** |

## Why K cannot distinguish them — the mechanism, not the symptom

**1. K validates the verb and never the detail. **`migrations/037_document_lifecycle_events.sql:34` states the contract in its own words:

> Verb-specific detail (e.g. rename's new display name, share-revoke's share id). **Free-form by design — the vocabulary owns the verb, S owns the detail.**

So on a `share-permission-change` row, whether the permission moved *to NoAccess* (a revoke) or from view→download (a routine change) lives entirely in a `payload JSONB` K neither schemas, validates nor documents. K has **no basis** to reclassify one as the other.

**2.** `share-revoke` **and** `share-permission-change` **are SEPARATE entries in K's own closed vocabulary** (`services/originate/src/lifecycleActions.ts:40-41`, `docs/VOCABULARY.md:45`). K already has a verb that means *revoked*. A revoke arriving as `share-permission-change` is therefore not merely under-detailed — it is **mislabelled against K's own contract**, and K's graph will read it as a permission edit forever.

**3. There is no gap detection, so an absent event is undetectable. **`document_lifecycle_events` holds `id, tenant_id, parent_document_id, action, payload, actor_user_id, anchor_id, created_at` — **no sequence number and no previous-event pointer**. Reads are *"events for this document, newest first"*. An event S never sends leaves no hole to notice.

**Worth flagging on its own:** migration 037's header says *"K's lineage view of these events now mirrors S's PreviousChainId chain." ***The schema does not do that.** It attaches events to `parent_document_id`; it stores no chain link between events. The comment claims a property the table cannot provide, and it is the property that would have made an omission detectable.

**4. No reconciliation exists.** The only reconciler in the tree is KS-584's **stuck-anchor** reconciler (`services/anchoring/src/reconciler.ts`) — it reconciles K's own anchor submission state against chain, not S's event stream against K's. Grep for `reconcil` across `Blockchain/Dev/services/` returns that and nothing else.

## Controls

* *The vocabulary grep can find things* — `share-permission-change` returns non-zero across 10 files, against `share-revoke`'s 20.
* *The absence of a sequence column is real, not a missed migration* — `037_…lifecycle_events.sql` is the only lifecycle migration in the tree, and no later migration adds one.
